Title: Assisted Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The assisted pull-up reduces effective bodyweight via a machine counterweight or band so trainees can practice full-ROM vertical pulling with proper scapular mechanics before unassisted pull-ups are possible.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Biceps and elbow flexors
- Rhomboids and trapezius
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Assisted pull-up/dip machine or heavy resistance band over a bar
- Pull-up bar

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Select assistance level that allows controlled full-ROM reps.
2. Grip the bar (pronated, neutral, or supinated as programmed).
3. Pull from a hang position to chin-over-bar with packed shoulders.
4. Lower under control.
5. Reduce assistance over weeks as capacity improves.

## Coaching Cues

- "Assistance allows quality, not laziness"
- "Full hang to chin clearance"
- "Pack the shoulders"
- "Lower slowly"

## Common Mistakes

- Too much assistance (no challenge)
- Too little assistance causing failed ugly reps
- Partial ROM
- Relying on bounce/kip

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Controlled hang to chin-over-bar.

## Progressions

- Less machine assistance or lighter band
- Unassisted pull-up
- Slow eccentrics with less help

## Regressions

- Higher assistance
- Lat pulldown
- Inverted row
- Scapular pull-up + negatives

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–150 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–3x weekly for beginners building pull-up capacity

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Allows productive vertical-pull volume before unassisted strength exists.

#### Strength

Skill and strength bridge to unassisted pull-ups.

#### Endurance

Easy to accumulate quality reps.

#### Fat Loss

Useful pulling option when fatigue is high.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Band-Assisted Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The band-assisted pull-up uses a looped resistance band to provide accommodating assistance (more help at the bottom, less near the top), bridging bodyweight vertical pulling skill and strength.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Elbow flexors
- Upper-back retractors
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar
- Heavy loop resistance band anchored securely over the bar
- Knee or foot in the band depending on setup

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Anchor the band safely over the bar; place a knee or foot into the loop.
2. Grip the bar and assume a packed hang.
3. Pull to chin-over-bar with minimal swing.
4. Lower under control against the band.
5. Progress by using a lighter band over time.

## Coaching Cues

- "Band is stable before you load it"
- "Strict pull"
- "Chin over, then control down"
- "Lighter band as you improve"

## Common Mistakes

- Unstable band setup (safety risk)
- Excessive kipping
- Band so heavy that top lockout has zero challenge
- Incomplete hang

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Hang to chin-over-bar.

## Progressions

- Lighter band
- Unassisted pull-up
- Pause at the top with band

## Regressions

- Heavier band
- Assisted machine
- Lat pulldown

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–150 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–3x weekly while building pull-ups

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Productive vertical-pull volume with accessible setup.

#### Strength

Progression tool toward unassisted pulling strength.

#### Endurance

Good for higher-rep practice.

#### Fat Loss

Convenient when a machine is unavailable.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Ensure band and anchor integrity before each set.

Title: Barbell Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

The barbell row is a bent-over horizontal pulling exercise that loads the upper and mid-back, lats, and elbow flexors while demanding isometric trunk and hip stability. It is a primary free-weight row for building pulling strength and back hypertrophy and pairs well with vertical pulls such as pulldowns or pull-ups.

## Primary Muscles

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius
- Posterior shoulder complex contributions based on elbow path

## Secondary Muscles

- Biceps brachii and other elbow flexors
- Rear delts
- Spinal erectors (isometric support)
- Abdominals / trunk stabilizers
- Glutes and hamstrings (isometric hip hinge support)

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Optional: lifting straps for high-rep sets when grip limits back loading
- Optional: rack setup for consistent starting height

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Benefits

- Compound horizontal-pull overload with measurable load progression
- Trains scapular retraction and elbow-driven pulling together
- Builds trunk stability under load when hinged position is maintained
- Complements vertical pulling for balanced back development

## Execution

1. Stand with feet roughly hip-to-shoulder width. Hinge at the hips to a torso angle that can be maintained (commonly ~15–45° above parallel, individualized).
2. Grip the bar just outside the legs. Brace the trunk; keep a neutral spine and soft knees.
3. Pull the bar toward the lower chest/upper abdomen by driving the elbows back while retracting the scapulae.
4. Pause briefly without turning the lift into a shrug-only or lumbar-extension finish.
5. Lower the bar under control toward full arm extension without losing the hinge position; repeat.

## Common Mistakes

- Standing too upright and converting the row into a partial shrug/curl
- Using hip drive and lumbar extension as the primary movers
- Rounding the thoracic/lumbar spine under fatigue
- Cutting ROM and never reaching a true stretch or contraction
- Excessively wide elbows that irritate the shoulders without improving back tension

## Coaching Cues

- “Hips back, spine long”
- “Pull elbows to the hips/ribs”
- “Squeeze the shoulder blades, don’t yank the bar”
- “Lower with control; stay hinged”

## Programming

Use as a primary horizontal pull on back, upper, or pull days. Strength-focused sets work well in lower-to-moderate reps with longer rests. Hypertrophy-focused sets benefit from strict torso position, controlled eccentrics, and 0–3 RIR. If lower-back fatigue limits quality, substitute chest-supported rows for some volume.

## Sets

- Strength focus: 3–5 sets
- Hypertrophy focus: 3–4 sets

Title: Barbell Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Reps

- Strength focus: 4–6 reps
- Hypertrophy focus: 6–12 reps

## Tempo

- 2-0-1-0 to 3-1-1-0

## Rest Time

- Strength focus: 2–3 minutes
- Hypertrophy focus: 90–180 seconds

## Variations

- Pendlay row
- Yates row (more upright torso)
- Underhand barbell row
- Chest-supported barbell or dumbbell row

## Regression

- Chest-supported row
- Seated cable row
- Dumbbell single-arm row

## Progression

- Progressive load increases
- Paused rows at peak contraction
- Slow eccentrics
- Pendlay resets for strength emphasis

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic low-back pain aggravated by hinging, recent lumbar injury, uncontrolled high blood pressure responses to heavy straining, or active biceps/elbow tendinopathy worsened by gripping and pulling. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Science Summary

Horizontal rowing exercises produce substantial activation of the latissimus dorsi and scapular retractors and are standard components of evidence-based resistance programs for upper-body pulling strength and hypertrophy. Free-weight bent-over rows add high trunk stability demand compared with supported machines, which can be beneficial for transfer but may limit load if spinal endurance fails first. Hand spacing and torso angle alter regional emphasis; no single row style is universally superior. Weekly pulling volume, progressive overload, and controlled technique predict adaptation better than attachment novelty.

B

Title: Cable Pullover | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The cable pullover (often kneeling or standing with a rope/bar from a high pulley) trains shoulder extension under continuous tension, isolating the lats more consistently than many free-weight pullover setups.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Teres major
- Triceps long head
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension
- Scapular depressors

## Equipment

- High cable
- Rope or bar
- Optional pad for kneeling

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Kneel or stand facing away/side-on depending on setup; hold the rope overhead with soft elbows.
2. Extend the shoulders to bring the rope toward the hips/thighs.
3. Squeeze the lats at the finish.
4. Return to a long stretch.
5. Keep elbows angle relatively fixed.

## Coaching Cues

- "Long arms"
- "Pull to the hips with the lats"
- "Ribs down"
- "Stretch back up"

## Common Mistakes

- Heavy elbow bend
- Lumbar flare
- Momentum
- Cutting the stretch

## Breathing

Exhale on the pull-down arc; inhale on the return.

## Range of Motion

Overhead stretch to hip-level contraction.

## Progressions

- Load
- Slow eccentrics
- Single-arm cable pullover

## Regressions

- Straight-arm pulldown with lighter stack
- Machine pullover
- Band pullover

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Continuous-tension lat isolation.

#### Strength

Not primary.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep friendly.

#### Fat Loss

Accessory after compounds.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Chest-Supported Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The chest-supported row (machine or bench-supported free weights) removes much of the lower-back demand from rowing, allowing focused loading of the upper and mid-back and lats with less systemic fatigue from hip hinging.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors

### Stabilizers

- Scapular stabilizers
- Minimal lumbar demand versus bent-over rows

## Equipment

- Chest-supported row machine, or incline bench with dumbbells/barbell
- Appropriate handles

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Set chest pad/bench so arms can hang freely at the bottom.
2. Grab handles or dumbbells; start at a full stretch.
3. Row by driving elbows back and retracting scapulae.
4. Lower under control to stretch.
5. Keep ribs against the pad—avoid peeling the chest off to cheat.

## Coaching Cues

- "Chest glued to the pad"
- "Elbows back"
- "Squeeze at the top"
- "Full stretch at the bottom"

## Common Mistakes

- Peeling the torso off the pad
- Shrugging
- Partial stretch
- Yanking with momentum

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full hang/stretch to strong retraction without lumbar compensation.

## Progressions

- Load
- Pauses
- Single-arm chest-supported row

## Regressions

- Lighter machine row
- Seated cable row with lighter load
- Band row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent high-quality back volume with lower spinal fatigue.

#### Strength

Secondary strength; great accessory volume tool.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep friendly.

#### Fat Loss

Useful when low-back fatigue is limiting.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Chin-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

The chin-up is a closed-chain vertical pull performed with a supinated (underhand) grip. Compared with a pronated pull-up, it typically increases elbow-flexor contribution while still heavily loading the latissimus dorsi and upper back. It is a foundational relative-strength and hypertrophy movement.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Elbow flexors (biceps brachii, brachialis) with elevated relative demand versus pronated pull-ups

### Secondary

- Rhomboids and middle trapezius
- Rear deltoids
- Brachioradialis

### Stabilizers

- Core musculature
- Scapular depressors and retractors
- Rotator cuff

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar
- Optional: chalk, straps (use judiciously), assistance band, or weight belt

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Hang from the bar with a supinated grip, hands roughly shoulder-width, arms extended, shoulders packed (not shrugged into the ears).
2. Initiate by depressing and retracting the scapulae, then pull the elbows down and back.
3. Continue until the chin clears the bar (or chest approaches the bar in advanced variations).
4. Lower under control to a full hang without losing shoulder packing.
5. Reset tension and repeat.

## Coaching Cues

- "Pack the shoulders, then pull"
- "Elbows to the ribs/pockets"
- "Chest up toward the bar"
- "Lower with control—no drop"

## Common Mistakes

- Kipping or excessive swing when strict reps are intended
- Incomplete ROM (chronic half-reps without programming intent)
- Shrugging into the neck at the bottom or top
- Flaring elbows without lat engagement
- Relying only on elbow flexion and losing scapular control

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

From a controlled dead hang to chin-over-bar (or chest-to-bar if capacity allows). Avoid painful end-range shoulder positions.

## Progressions

- Weighted chin-ups
- Slow eccentrics / paused reps at the top
- Chest-to-bar chin-ups
- L-sit chin-ups (advanced trunk demand)

## Regressions

- Band-assisted chin-up
- Machine-assisted chin-up
- Negative-only chin-ups
- Underhand lat pulldown

## Programming

### Sets

- Strength: 3–5 sets
- Hypertrophy: 3–4 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 3–6
- Hypertrophy: 6–12 (use assistance or added load to stay in range)

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3 for most working sets

### Rest

- Strength: 2–4 minutes
- Hypertrophy: 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 sessions weekly within total vertical-pull volume

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent vertical-pull hypertrophy stimulus with strong biceps contribution.

#### Strength

High-value relative-strength builder; progress with added load once bodyweight sets are solid.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep sets possible with assistance or strong trainees.

#### Fat Loss

Keep as a primary pull if technique holds under fatigue; otherwise use pulldowns.

Title: Close-Grip Lat Pulldown | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The close-grip lat pulldown uses a narrow attachment (often V-bar or close pronated/neutral grip), typically increasing elbow-flexor involvement and allowing a strong contraction at the bottom of the vertical pull.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Biceps brachii and brachialis
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular stabilizers
- Core against pad

## Equipment

- Lat pulldown station
- V-bar or close-grip handle
- Thigh pad

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Attach a close-grip handle; secure thighs.
2. Start tall with arms extended.
3. Pull the handle to the upper chest/sternum while elbows track down and back.
4. Squeeze briefly; return to a full stretch.
5. Keep ribs down—avoid excessive lumbar arching.

## Coaching Cues

- "Pull to the chest"
- "Elbows to pockets"
- "Stretch tall at the top"
- "No bounce"

## Common Mistakes

- Turning into a biceps-only curl
- Cutting the overhead stretch
- Extreme lean and momentum
- Shrugging the finish

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full stretch overhead to a controlled peak contraction at the chest.

## Progressions

- Load
- Slow eccentrics
- Neutral-grip pull-ups

## Regressions

- Higher seat assistance via lighter load
- Assisted pull-up
- Seated cable row for horizontal volume

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Strong lat + elbow-flexor vertical-pull option.

#### Strength

Useful accessory for pulling strength.

#### Endurance

Higher reps suitable.

#### Fat Loss

Good machine compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Dumbbell Pullover | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The dumbbell pullover is performed lying across or along a bench while moving a dumbbell through a large shoulder-extension arc. It loads the latissimus dorsi (and can involve the chest depending on technique), providing a stretch-biased upper-body accessory.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Pectoralis major (technique-dependent)
- Triceps long head
- Serratus anterior (stabilizing role)

### Stabilizers

- Core against lumbar extension
- Shoulder stabilizers
- Glutes if bridging across the bench

## Equipment

- Dumbbell
- Flat bench
- Optional: lie along the bench for more support

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Lie along or perpendicular to a bench holding a dumbbell over the chest with arms softly bent.
2. Lower the dumbbell overhead into a deep comfortable stretch while keeping ribs from flaring excessively.
3. Pull the dumbbell back over the chest using the lats (and pecs as involved).
4. Maintain a consistent soft elbow angle.
5. Use conservative ROM if shoulders feel pinched.

## Coaching Cues

- "Soft elbows fixed"
- "Stretch without dumping the ribs"
- "Pull with the armpits/lats"
- "Do not turn it into a skull crusher"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive lumbar extension
- Too much elbow bend (skull-crusher pattern)
- Painful end-range forcing
- Unstable dumbbell grip

## Breathing

Inhale into the stretch; exhale as you pull back over the chest.

## Range of Motion

Deep overhead stretch within shoulder comfort to dumbbell-over-chest finish.

## Progressions

- Slightly heavier load with control
- Cable pullover for continuous tension
- Tempo stretches

## Regressions

- Straight-arm pulldown
- Machine pullover
- Shorter ROM pullover

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 2–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Stretch-biased lat (and sometimes pec) accessory.

#### Strength

Not primary.

#### Endurance

Light higher reps possible.

#### Fat Loss

Optional accessory.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Avoid aggressive end ranges with shoulder irritation.

Title: Dumbbell Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The dumbbell row is a unilateral bent-over or supported horizontal pull that loads the latissimus dorsi and upper back through a large ROM, while allowing natural shoulder pathing and side-to-side balancing.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Spinal erectors (depending on support)

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-rotation
- Glute/hip of the stance leg
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Dumbbell
- Flat bench for hand/knee support (common)
- Optional: free staggered stance without bench

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Place one hand and ipsilateral knee on a bench (or hinge with free hand braced).
2. Hold the dumbbell in the opposite hand, arm hanging long, spine neutral.
3. Row the elbow toward the hip/back pocket.
4. Lower to a deep stretch without rotating the pelvis excessively.
5. Complete reps, then switch sides.

## Coaching Cues

- "Elbow to hip"
- "Neutral spine"
- "Reach long at the bottom"
- "Do not yank with the torso"

## Common Mistakes

- Rotating and heaving the torso
- Shrugging the dumbbell
- Short ROM
- Rounding the low back

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full stretch hang to elbow-back contraction near the torso.

## Progressions

- Heavier dumbbells
- Kroc-style higher-rep heavy sets
- Pauses
- Meadows row

## Regressions

- Chest-supported dumbbell row
- Cable single-arm row
- Machine row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets per side

### Reps

- Hypertrophy: 8–15
- Strength-biased: 6–10

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Cornerstone unilateral back hypertrophy exercise.

#### Strength

Builds unilateral pulling strength.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep Kroc-style sets possible for advanced trainees.

#### Fat Loss

Time-efficient unilateral compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Face Pull | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The face pull is a cable or band exercise pulling toward the face with external rotation bias, targeting the rear deltoids, rhomboids, and external rotators. It is widely used for upper-back balance and shoulder-health accessory work alongside heavier vertical and horizontal pulls.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Rear deltoids
- Rhomboids and middle/lower trapezius

### Secondary

- Infraspinatus and teres minor (external rotation component)
- Biceps (minor)

### Stabilizers

- Scapular stabilizers
- Core in standing variations

## Equipment

- Cable set at upper-chest/face height
- Rope attachment
- Optional band alternative

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Set cable high; grip rope ends with thumbs toward yourself.
2. Step back into tension; start arms long.
3. Pull the rope toward the face/forehead while externally rotating so fists end near ears.
4. Squeeze rear delts/upper back; return under control.
5. Avoid shrugging into the neck or flaring into a pure upright row.

## Coaching Cues

- "Rope to face, knuckles back"
- "Elbows high but controlled"
- "Externally rotate at the finish"
- "No shrug"

## Common Mistakes

- Turning into an upright row with internal rotation
- Excessive load
- Lumbar lean cheating
- Ending with elbows low and no upper-back squeeze

## Breathing

Exhale on the pull; inhale on the return.

## Range of Motion

Arms long under tension to face-level finish with external rotation.

## Progressions

- Load within control
- Pauses at peak external rotation
- Single-arm face pull

## Regressions

- Band face pull
- Rear-delt fly light
- Prone Y/T raises

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 12–20

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3; technique priority

### Rest

- 45–75 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–4x weekly as accessory

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Upper-back/rear-delt accessory volume.

#### Strength

Not a primary strength lift.

#### Endurance

Excellent higher-rep option.

#### Fat Loss

Low-fatigue shoulder-balance work.

## Contraindications

Reduce load/ROM if shoulder pain appears. Not medical diagnosis.

Title: Feet-Elevated Inverted Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The feet-elevated inverted row increases the difficulty of the bodyweight horizontal pull by raising the feet, shifting more load through the upper body and increasing demand on the lats and upper back.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension
- Glutes
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Bar or rings
- Stable bench/box for feet
- Bodyweight

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set hands on the bar; place heels on an elevation so the body is nearer horizontal or decline.
2. Maintain a rigid plank.
3. Pull the chest to the bar; lower to full extension.
4. Avoid piking to cheat.
5. Progress elevation gradually.

## Coaching Cues

- "Heels up, body tight"
- "Chest to bar"
- "No pike"
- "Full stretch at the bottom"

## Common Mistakes

- Elevation too high too soon
- Hip sag/pike
- Partial depth
- Unstable foot surface

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full extension to chest-to-bar.

## Progressions

- Higher elevation
- Weighted vest
- Ring feet-elevated rows

## Regressions

- Standard inverted row
- Higher bar angle
- Cable row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 5–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–150 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Harder bodyweight horizontal-pull progression.

#### Strength

Relative strength builder.

#### Endurance

Use lower elevation for higher reps.

#### Fat Loss

Effective when equipment is limited.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Gorilla Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The gorilla row is a hinged double-dumbbell row alternating sides from a wide stance, combining bilateral hinge bracing with unilateral rowing for lat and mid-back stimulus plus anti-rotation demand.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Spinal erectors (isometric hinge)

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-rotation in the hinge
- Hip hinge stabilizers

## Equipment

- Pair of dumbbells
- Flat floor

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Hinge with a wide stance holding two dumbbells hanging below the shoulders.
2. Row one dumbbell to the hip while the other stays long as a counterbalance.
3. Lower and alternate sides.
4. Keep hips square and spine neutral.
5. Use loads that preserve the hinge.

## Coaching Cues

- "Stay hinged"
- "Alternate elbows to hips"
- "Hips quiet"
- "Long arm counterbalance"

## Common Mistakes

- Standing up out of the hinge
- Rotating the pelvis
- Rounding the back
- Short ROM

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Long hang to hip-height row finish each side.

## Progressions

- Heavier DBs
- Pause each side
- Slow eccentrics

## Regressions

- Supported single-arm DB row
- Seated cable row
- Chest-supported row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–12 per side

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Time-efficient unilateral/bilateral hybrid row.

#### Strength

Secondary.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Efficient if hinge quality holds.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Helms Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The Helms row is an elbow-flared, upper-back-biased dumbbell row typically performed chest-supported on an incline bench, emphasizing scapular retraction and rear-delt/upper-back stimulus with a stretch at the bottom.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Rhomboids and middle trapezius
- Rear deltoids
- Latissimus dorsi (still involved)

### Secondary

- Elbow flexors
- Posterior shoulder musculature

### Stabilizers

- Scapular stabilizers against the bench

## Equipment

- Adjustable incline bench
- Pair of dumbbells

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set a moderate incline; lie chest-down holding dumbbells.
2. Let arms hang with a stretch; elbows relatively flared versus a hip-oriented row.
3. Row by retracting scapulae and pulling elbows out/back toward the upper torso.
4. Squeeze upper back; lower into the stretch.
5. Keep chest on the pad.

## Coaching Cues

- "Chest on the pad"
- "Flare and retract"
- "Stretch the upper back"
- "Squeeze at the top"

## Common Mistakes

- Turning into a hip-driven row
- Peeling off the pad
- Using too much load and losing stretch
- Shrugging into the neck

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Deep stretch at the bottom to strong upper-back contraction.

## Progressions

- Load
- Tempo stretches
- Wide-grip cable row pairings

## Regressions

- Chest-supported machine row
- Face-pull
- Lighter standard DB row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Upper-back and rear-delt biased row variation.

#### Strength

Not a primary strength lift.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep suitable.

#### Fat Loss

Accessory volume tool.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Inverted Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The inverted row is a closed-chain horizontal pull performed under a bar or suspension trainer. It builds upper-back and lat strength with scalable bodyweight loading and is a key progression toward pull-ups for many beginners.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Posterior chain as a plank-like stabilizer

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension musculature
- Glutes
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Smith bar, rack bar, or rings/TRX set at appropriate height
- Stable floor surface

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Set a bar at about waist-to-hip height; hang underneath with a straight body plank from heels to head.
2. Pack the shoulders; pull the chest toward the bar.
3. Squeeze scapulae at the top.
4. Lower under control to full arm extension.
5. Keep hips from sagging or piking.

## Coaching Cues

- "Body in one line"
- "Chest to bar"
- "Pack, then pull"
- "Hips do not sag"

## Common Mistakes

- Hip sag turning it into a shrug-hang
- Partial ROM
- Leading with the head only
- Bar set so high that stimulus disappears

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Arms fully extended under tension to chest-near-bar contraction.

## Progressions

- Lower the bar / elevate feet
- Weighted vest
- Pause at the top
- Ring inverted rows

## Regressions

- Higher bar angle (more upright)
- Bent-knee inverted row
- Seated cable row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent bodyweight horizontal-pull hypertrophy tool.

#### Strength

Builds relative pulling strength toward pull-ups.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep accessible.

#### Fat Loss

Great minimal-equipment pull.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Kroc Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The Kroc row is a high-effort, high-rep unilateral dumbbell row performed with heavier loads and some controlled body English historically used for upper-back thickness, grip, and work capacity. Modern coaching still prioritizes a relatively stable spine and full ROM.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle/upper trapezius

### Secondary

- Elbow flexors
- Rear deltoids
- Grip/forearm musculature

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-rotation
- Hip hinge support
- Grip endurance

## Equipment

- Heavy dumbbell
- Bench for support
- Optional straps (debate: use based on grip goals)

## Difficulty

advanced

## Execution

1. Brace one arm on a bench; hinge with a neutral spine.
2. Row a challenging dumbbell for higher reps, allowing minimal controlled momentum only if positions stay safe.
3. Emphasize a long stretch and strong finish each rep.
4. Stop if lumbar rounding or uncontrolled twisting appears.
5. Match both sides over the week if asymmetry is a concern.

## Coaching Cues

- "Heavy but controlled"
- "Long stretch"
- "Spine stays neutral"
- "Earn the reps—do not flop"

## Common Mistakes

- Sacrificing spinal position for load
- Uncontrolled twisting
- Partial stretch every rep
- Ego loading without warm-up sets

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Deep stretch to elbow-back finish; maintain quality under fatigue.

## Progressions

- Heavier dumbbells
- Higher quality-rep targets
- Less strap reliance if grip is a goal

## Regressions

- Standard moderated DB row
- Chest-supported row
- Cable single-arm row

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets per side

### Reps

- 10–20+ challenging reps

### Intensity

- High effort; RIR ~0–2 on final sets

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1x weekly per side emphasis for most

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

High-stimulus unilateral overload method when recovered.

#### Strength

Builds grip and pulling work capacity.

#### Endurance

Inherently endurance-biased within strength work.

#### Fat Loss

Demanding; manage recovery carefully.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Not ideal for beginners or those with uncontrolled back pain.

Title: Landmine Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

Title: Lat Pulldown | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

The lat pulldown is a machine- or cable-based vertical pulling exercise that loads the latissimus dorsi with meaningful contribution from the biceps, rear delts, and other upper-back muscles. It is commonly used to build pulling strength and back hypertrophy when pull-ups are not yet accessible, and as a volume tool alongside bodyweight vertical pulls.

## Primary Muscles

- Latissimus dorsi
- Upper-back synergists (depending on grip and torso angle), including teres major

## Secondary Muscles

- Biceps brachii
- Rear delts / posterior shoulder complex
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius (scapular control)
- Brachialis and brachioradialis (grip-dependent)

## Equipment

- Lat pulldown station or high cable with appropriate attachment
- Common attachments: straight bar, wide bar, neutral-grip handles

## Difficulty

beginner

## Benefits

- Scalable vertical-pull loading for beginners through advanced trainees
- Useful hypertrophy stimulus for the lats when progressed with sufficient tension and ROM
- Easier load prescription than bodyweight pull-ups
- Grip and attachment options can accommodate shoulder comfort differences

## Execution

1. Adjust the thigh pad so the torso stays seated during the pull. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width unless using a specific variation.
2. Start with arms extended overhead and a slight forward lean if needed for a full stretch without excessive lumbar sway.
3. Initiate by depressing and retracting the scapulae, then pull the elbows down and back until the bar approaches the upper chest.
4. Pause briefly with control at the bottom without shrugging or yanking.
5. Return the bar under control to full elbow extension while keeping the ribs stacked and shoulders stable.

## Common Mistakes

- Using momentum and leaning excessively to finish reps
- Pulling behind the neck, which can increase shoulder stress for many lifters
- Ending the ROM at the face and never reaching a meaningful lat contraction
- Over-shrugging at the top and losing scapular control
- Excessively wide grips that reduce effective ROM and increase discomfort

## Coaching Cues

- “Drive elbows to the back pockets”
- “Chest up, ribs down”
- “Long arms at the top; controlled pull to the chest”
- “Own the eccentric”

## Programming

Use as a primary vertical pull for beginners or as accessory volume after pull-ups/chin-ups. For hypertrophy, train in moderate rep ranges with controlled eccentrics and leave roughly 0–3 RIR. Pair with a horizontal row for balanced back development.

## Sets

- 3–4 sets

Title: Lat Pulldown | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Reps

- 8–12 reps (hypertrophy default)
- 6–8 reps for heavier strength-biased sets

## Tempo

- 2-0-1-0 to 3-1-1-0

## Rest Time

- 90–150 seconds

## Variations

- Neutral-grip lat pulldown
- Close-grip lat pulldown
- Single-arm cable pulldown
- Wide-grip lat pulldown

## Regression

- Assisted pull-up machine with higher assistance
- Band-assisted flexible pulldown pattern
- Seated cable row (if vertical pulling is poorly tolerated)

## Progression

- Heavier load with unchanged ROM
- Slow eccentrics
- Single-arm overload
- Transition toward pull-up variations

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement during overhead positions, recent lat or biceps strain, or elbow tendinopathy aggravated by pulling. Behind-the-neck variations are often poorly tolerated and are usually unnecessary. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Science Summary

Vertical pulling exercises meaningfully activate the latissimus dorsi and elbow flexors. Lat pulldowns allow precise external loading and can produce similar regional back development goals as pull-ups when effort and volume are matched sufficiently, though the kinetic chain and stability demands differ. Grip width and orientation change muscle emphasis and joint stress more than they create unique “must-do” patterns; front pulldowns to the chest are generally preferred over behind-the-neck versions for comfort and practical ROM. Progressive overload and weekly pulling volume remain the primary drivers of hypertrophy.

B

Title: Negative Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The negative pull-up emphasizes the eccentric phase by starting at the top (jump or step to chin-over-bar) and lowering slowly. Eccentric-focused practice builds pull-up strength and control when concentric pull-ups are not yet achievable.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Elbow flexors
- Rhomboids and trapezius
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar
- Box or step to reach the top position
- Optional band for partial assistance

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Step or jump to a chin-over-bar position with shoulders packed.
2. Lower for a prescribed tempo (often 3–5+ seconds) to a full hang.
3. Drop or step down safely; reset for the next rep.
4. Keep the body from uncontrolled falling.
5. Stop if scapular control is lost.

## Coaching Cues

- "Start strong at the top"
- "Fight the descent"
- "Shoulders packed all the way down"
- "Smooth, not a freefall"

## Common Mistakes

- Dropping too fast
- Losing packing and dumping into the shoulders
- Too many hard eccentrics causing excessive soreness without recovery
- Incomplete top starting position

## Breathing

Inhale and brace at the top; controlled exhale during the slow descent as needed.

## Range of Motion

Chin-over-bar start to controlled full hang.

## Progressions

- Longer eccentric times
- Pause mid-ROM
- Assisted concentric + negative
- Full pull-up

## Regressions

- Shorter eccentrics
- Lat pulldown slow eccentrics
- Inverted row slow lowers

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- 3–6 slow negatives

### Intensity

- High effort; leave recovery buffer (not daily maxing)

### Rest

- 2–3 minutes

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly depending on recovery

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Eccentric loading can support hypertrophy while building pull-up capacity.

#### Strength

Key bridge for pull-up strength development.

#### Endurance

Not ideal as high-rep endurance work.

#### Fat Loss

Use sparingly if sore; prefer pulldowns when fatigued.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. Title: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The neutral-grip pull-up uses a parallel (palms-facing) grip, often feeling more shoulder- and elbow-friendly than fully pronated or supinated variations while still loading the lats, upper back, and elbow flexors.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Biceps brachii and brachialis
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core musculature
- Scapular stabilizers
- Rotator cuff

## Equipment

- Neutral-grip pull-up handles or parallel bars
- Optional assistance or weight belt

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Grip neutral handles; hang with arms extended and shoulders packed.
2. Depress/retract scapulae, then pull elbows down.
3. Raise until chin clears the handles.
4. Lower under control to a full hang.
5. Minimize swing unless kipping is intentionally programmed.

## Coaching Cues

- "Palms face each other"
- "Pull elbows to pockets"
- "Pack, then pull"
- "Quiet body, strict reps"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive swinging
- Partial ROM
- Shrugging
- Neck craning over the bar without scapular control

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Dead hang to chin-over-handles with controlled scapular motion.

## Progressions

- Weighted neutral-grip pull-ups
- Slow eccentrics
- Chest-to-bar neutral pulls

## Regressions

- Assisted neutral-grip pull-up
- Neutral-grip lat pulldown
- Inverted row with neutral handles

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- 4–12 depending on goal and assistance/load

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds (up to 3–4 minutes for heavy weighted sets)

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Joint-friendly vertical pull for lat and upper-back volume.

#### Strength

Strong relative-strength option when pronated grip irritates tissues.

#### Endurance

Assistance enables higher-rep work.

#### Fat Loss

Solid primary pull when recovered.

Title: Pendlay Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The Pendlay row is a strict bent-over barbell row performed from a dead stop on the floor each rep. Removing stretch-reflex contribution emphasizes explosive upper-back/lat force production and technique discipline.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Spinal erectors (isometric hinge)

### Stabilizers

- Core bracing in the hinge
- Scapular stabilizers
- Grip

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Plates that allow the bar to rest at mid-shin height
- Clear floor space

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set a hip hinge with the bar over mid-foot; grip like a deadlift/row hybrid.
2. Brace; pull the bar explosively to the lower chest/upper abdomen.
3. Lower under control to a full dead stop on the floor.
4. Reset tightness every rep—do not bounce.
5. Maintain a consistent torso angle near parallel when possible.

## Coaching Cues

- "Dead stop every rep"
- "Explode to the torso"
- "Stay hinged"
- "Reset before the next pull"

## Common Mistakes

- Touch-and-go bouncing
- Standing up out of the hinge
- Rounding the back
- Pulling too high into a shrug

## Breathing

Brace and brief hold before the pull; exhale as the bar reaches the torso or after the rep.

## Range of Motion

Floor dead stop to torso contact; full reset between reps.

## Progressions

- Heavier loads
- Paused at the torso
- Deficit Pendlay if mobility allows

## Regressions

- Chest-supported row
- Seal row
- Lighter conventional barbell row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 3–6
- Hypertrophy: 5–8

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 2–4 minutes

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Useful for strict, high-tension row volume.

#### Strength

Excellent explosive row strength builder.

#### Endurance

Not ideal.

#### Fat Loss

Use lighter technique work if fatigued.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Overview

The plate-loaded row (often iso-lateral) allows independent arm loading on a guided path, combining heavy overload potential with machine stability for lat and mid-back development.

1. Set seat so arms reach a full stretch at the bottom.

## Overview

## Overview

The prone trap raise (prone Y raise) is a light upper-back and lower-trapezius accessory performed face-down, raising the arms into a Y pattern to improve scapular control and balance heavy pulling programs.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Lower trapezius
- Middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Rotator cuff musculature

### Stabilizers

- Scapular stabilizers
- Core against the bench

## Equipment

- Incline or flat bench
- Very light dumbbells or no load

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Lie prone on an incline/flat bench holding light dumbbells.
2. Raise arms into a Y overhead while depressing/retracting scapulae.
3. Keep thumbs up; avoid shrugging into the ears aggressively.
4. Lower under control.
5. Prioritize crisp scapular motion over load.

## Coaching Cues

- "Light weight, perfect scapulae"
- "Thumbs up into a Y"
- "Long neck"
- "Squeeze lower traps"

## Common Mistakes

- Too much load
- Turning into a shrug-heavy pattern
- Bending elbows excessively
- Neck strain from looking up hard

## Breathing

Exhale on the raise; inhale on the lower.

## Range of Motion

Arms hang under control to an overhead Y without pain.

## Progressions

- Slightly heavier micro-loads
- Longer pauses
- Face-pull pairings

## Regressions

- No-load prone Y
- Band pull-aparts
- Scapular drills on rings

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–3 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- Technique-focused RIR 2–4

### Rest

- 45–75 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–3x weekly as accessory

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Small muscle accessory; supports upper-back balance.

#### Strength

Scapular control for pulling strength.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep suitable.

#### Fat Loss

Low-fatigue accessory.

## Contraindications

Stop if shoulder pain appears; reduce ROM/load. Not medical advice.

Title: Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

The pull-up is a closed-chain vertical pulling exercise performed from a dead hang to chin-over-bar (or chest-to-bar in advanced variations). It heavily loads the latissimus dorsi and upper-back musculature with substantial elbow-flexor involvement. It is a foundational relative-strength movement and an effective hypertrophy tool when volume and progression are programmed deliberately.

## Primary Muscles

- Latissimus dorsi
- Upper-back synergists (teres major, rhomboids, trapezius involvement based on scapular action)

## Secondary Muscles

- Biceps brachii
- Brachialis and brachioradialis
- Rear delts
- Core stabilizers

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar or stable overhead handle
- Optional: resistance bands, assisted machine, weight belt/vest for progression

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Benefits

- High-transfer vertical pulling strength relative to bodyweight
- Effective lat and upper-back stimulus when full ROM is used
- Minimal equipment requirement
- Clear progression path via assistance, tempo, and added load

## Execution

1. Grip the bar with an overhand (pronated) grip, commonly slightly wider than shoulder width. Start from a dead hang with active shoulders (not passively shrugged into the ears).
2. Brace the trunk lightly. Initiate by depressing the scapulae, then pull the elbows down and toward the ribs.
3. Continue until the chin clears the bar without excessive cervical jutting or kipping.
4. Lower under control to full elbow extension.
5. Reset tension and repeat; avoid swinging between reps unless using an intentional kipping variation outside strict strength/hypertrophy work.

## Common Mistakes

- Partial reps that never reach a true hang or chin clearance
- Excessive kipping and momentum in strength/hypertrophy sets
- Shrugging to the ears and yanking with the arms only
- Overextending the lumbar spine to “finish” the rep
- Starting beyond current capacity and reinforcing poor ROM

## Coaching Cues

- “Pack the shoulders, then pull”
- “Elbows to the ribs”
- “Chest toward the bar”
- “Lower all the way without losing control”

## Programming

Use as a primary vertical pull when technique is solid. Beginners should prefer assisted variations or lat pulldowns until several strict reps are available. For hypertrophy, accumulate quality sets near technical failure. For strength, emphasize lower-rep sets, controlled eccentrics, and eventual weighted progressions.

## Sets

- Strength focus: 3–5 sets
- Hypertrophy focus: 3–4 sets

## Reps

- Strength focus: 3–6 strict reps
- Hypertrophy focus: 6–12 reps (use assistance or added load to stay in range)

## Tempo

- 2-0-1-0 to 3-1-1-0
- Optional paused top or bottom positions for control

Title: Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Rest Time

- Strength focus: 2–4 minutes
- Hypertrophy focus: 90–180 seconds

## Variations

- Chin-up (supinated)
- Neutral-grip pull-up
- Band-assisted pull-up
- Weighted pull-up
- Eccentric-only pull-up

## Regression

- Band-assisted pull-up
- Assisted pull-up machine
- Lat pulldown
- Foot-assisted eccentric pull-ups

## Progression

- Reduce assistance
- Add a weight belt or vest
- Slow eccentrics / paused reps
- Chest-to-bar strict pull-ups

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder pain in overhead hanging positions, recent elbow flexor or lat strain, or acute grip injury. Abrupt high-volume pull-up work can aggravate medial elbow or shoulder tissues in underprepared trainees. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Science Summary

Pull-ups elicit high activation of the latissimus dorsi and elbow flexors and are supported as effective upper-body pulling exercises for strength and muscle development. Grip orientation shifts relative biceps versus lat emphasis but does not invalidate any standard variation when ROM and effort are equated. Compared with lat pulldowns, pull-ups impose greater relative-load and stability demands; both can contribute to hypertrophy when progressive overload is applied. Assistance and eccentric-focused strategies are evidence-consistent ways to build capacity before full strict sets.

Title: Rack Pull | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The rack pull is a partial-range deadlift variation starting from pins/blocks above the floor (often below or above the knee). It overloads the upper back, traps, grip, and lockout portion of the hinge while reducing demand from the floor pull.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Spinal erectors
- Trapezius and upper back
- Latissimus dorsi (stabilizing/pulling the bar into the body)

### Secondary

- Gluteus maximus and hamstrings (depending on start height)
- Grip/forearm musculature
- Quadriceps contribution varies with height

### Stabilizers

- Core bracing musculature
- Scapular depressors/retractors
- Hip stabilizers

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Power rack with safety pins or sturdy blocks
- Optional straps depending on grip goals

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set pins at the desired height; place the bar on the pins.
2. Hinge and grip; pack the back and brace as in a deadlift.
3. Drive to lockout by extending hips and knees; stand tall without hyperextending the lumbar spine.
4. Lower under control to the pins; reset each rep (or touch-and-go if programmed).
5. Keep the bar close to the body.

## Coaching Cues

- "Brace before it leaves the pins"
- "Bar close"
- "Stand tall—do not lean back"
- "Reset tightness each rep"

## Common Mistakes

- Starting height so high it becomes a pointless shrug
- Hyperextending the low back at lockout
- Rounded thoracic/lumbar positions under maximal loads
- Bouncing violently off pins

## Breathing

Brace with a breath before the pull; exhale at lockout or between reps as appropriate for heavy sets.

## Range of Motion

From pin height to full hip extension lockout; intentionally partial versus floor deadlift.

## Progressions

- Heavier loads
- Lower pin heights toward floor pulls
- Paused lockouts

## Regressions

- Higher pins with lighter technique focus
- Chest-supported rows for upper-back volume
- Trap-bar deadlift if available (legs folder)

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 3–5
- Hypertrophy/overload: 5–8

### Intensity

- Often heavy; RIR 1–3 with conservative spinal positions

### Rest

- 2–5 minutes

### Frequency

- 1x weekly for most

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Overload stimulus for upper back/traps and posterior chain lockout.

#### Strength

Common lockout and overload strength tool.

#### Endurance

Not ideal.

#### Fat Loss

Demanding; reduce frequency in deficits.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. High spinal loading—use conservative progression and technique standards.

Title: Renegade Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The renegade row is a plank-based alternating dumbbell row that combines horizontal pulling with high anti-rotation and anti-extension core demand. Back loading is typically lighter than dedicated rows because stability limits the weight.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids (moderate loads)

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Core anti-rotation musculature (high demand)

### Stabilizers

- Full plank chain: abs, glutes, shoulders
- Base-side shoulder stabilizers

## Equipment

- Pair of hexagonal dumbbells (preferred for stability)
- Flat floor

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Assume a plank on two dumbbells, feet wide for stability.
2. Row one dumbbell to the hip while keeping hips square.
3. Lower it; alternate sides.
4. Minimize rotation and hip sway.
5. Use loads that preserve plank quality.

## Coaching Cues

- "Wide feet, tight plank"
- "Hips stay quiet"
- "Elbow to hip"
- "Light enough to own the position"

## Common Mistakes

- Rotating the pelvis each rep
- Sagging lumbar spine
- Ego loading
- Hands on round dumbbells that roll (safety)

## Breathing

Exhale on each row; maintain brace throughout.

## Range of Motion

Arm long on the floor support side; working arm to hip-height row finish.

## Progressions

- Heavier DBs within control
- Pause at the top
- Narrower feet (harder anti-rotation)

## Regressions

- Plank with single-arm DB row hand on bench
- Standard dumbbell row
- Bird-dog row regressions

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–10 per side

### Intensity

- RIR 2–4 (stability-limited)

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Secondary back stimulus; more core-stability hybrid.

#### Strength

Anti-rotation strength emphasis.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Conditioning-friendly hybrid if technique holds.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Avoid if plank positions aggravate wrists/shoulders/low back.

## Overview

beginner

2. Start with arms extended.
3. Pull the bar to the upper chest with elbows tracking down/back.

5. Avoid excessive lumbar arching.

- "Underhand, elbows to ribs"
- "Bar to chest"

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

Full overhead stretch to upper-chest contact.

- 3–4 sets

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

Lat + biceps biased vertical pull.

#### Strength

Accessory toward chin-up strength.

#### Endurance

Higher reps OK if elbows tolerate.

Useful machine compound.

## Contraindications

Title: Ring Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The ring row is an inverted row performed on gymnastic rings, adding instability that increases demand on scapular stabilizers, grip, and trunk control while training the lats and upper back.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Serratus/scapular stabilizers

### Stabilizers

- Rotator cuff
- Core anti-extension
- Grip

## Equipment

- Gymnastic rings or suspension trainer
- Stable anchors
- Adjustable strap length for difficulty

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set rings at an appropriate height; hold and lean back into a plank.
2. Pack shoulders; pull rings toward the ribcage/chest.
3. Squeeze scapulae; keep rings stable.
4. Lower to full arm extension under control.
5. Shorten straps or walk feet forward to progress.

## Coaching Cues

- "Break the rings apart lightly"
- "Body rigid"
- "Pull rings to ribs"
- "Quiet rings"

## Common Mistakes

- Sagging hips
- Letting rings crash inward without control
- Partial ROM
- Angle so easy stimulus is minimal

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full extension to strong retraction/pull.

## Progressions

- More horizontal body angle
- Feet elevated
- Pause reps
- Archer ring rows (advanced)

## Regressions

- More upright angle
- Bar inverted row
- Seated cable row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

High-quality unstable horizontal pull.

#### Strength

Builds stability and relative strength.

#### Endurance

Adjust angle for higher reps.

#### Fat Loss

Portable pulling option.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Scapular Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The scapular pull-up is a partial-range drill performed from a dead hang by depressing and retracting the scapulae without bending the elbows. It teaches shoulder packing and initiates lat engagement for pull-up progressions and scapular control.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi (initiation)
- Lower trapezius and scapular depressors

### Secondary

- Rhomboids
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Rotator cuff
- Core (light)

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Hang with arms straight and relaxed shoulders (active awareness, not pain).
2. Without bending elbows, depress and retract the scapulae to lift the body slightly.
3. Hold briefly at the packed position.
4. Return to a controlled hang.
5. Repeat for crisp, small-range reps.

## Coaching Cues

- "Long arms, move the shoulder blades"
- "Pockets the shoulders down"
- "No elbow bend"
- "Quiet, precise reps"

## Common Mistakes

- Bending the elbows into a mini pull-up
- Shrugging up instead of depressing
- Using momentum
- Overdoing volume with irritated shoulders

## Breathing

Exhale into the pack; inhale as you return to hang.

## Range of Motion

Small vertical displacement via scapular motion only; elbows remain extended.

## Progressions

- Longer pauses
- Add to pull-up freestanding sets as primers
- Full pull-up progression

## Regressions

- Scapular setting on an inverted row
- Band-assisted scapular pulls
- Prone scapular retraction drills

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- Technique-focused; RIR not primary

### Rest

- 45–75 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–4x weekly as a primer or skill drill

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Accessory/skill; not a primary mass builder.

#### Strength

Improves pull-up initiation mechanics.

#### Endurance

Can be used in warm-ups.

#### Fat Loss

Low-cost primer before pulling.

## Contraindications

Avoid if hanging aggravates shoulders; use supported regressions. Not medical advice.

Title: Seal Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The seal row is a chest-supported free-weight row performed lying prone on a raised bench so the weights hang freely. It minimizes momentum and lumbar involvement while heavily loading the back musculature.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors

### Stabilizers

- Scapular stabilizers
- Minimal hip/lumbar contribution

## Equipment

- Sturdy elevated bench or seal-row station
- Barbell or dumbbells
- Plates that can pass under the bench

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Lie prone on an elevated bench; grip barbell or dumbbells hanging below.
2. Row the load toward the bench/torso by driving elbows up/back.
3. Squeeze scapulae at the top.
4. Lower to a full stretch without bouncing plates off the floor (adjust bench height).
5. Keep thighs/chest supported throughout.

## Coaching Cues

- "Body stays quiet on the bench"
- "Elbows to the ceiling"
- "Stretch at the bottom"
- "No hip drive"

## Common Mistakes

- Bench too low causing floor bang every rep
- Using hip thrust to move weight
- Partial ROM
- Jerky reps

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full hang stretch to elbows-back contraction.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Paused seal rows
- Tempo eccentrics

## Regressions

- Chest-supported machine row
- Incline dumbbell row with torso on pad
- Seated cable row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–150 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

High-tension back builder with strict form.

#### Strength

Useful strict row strength.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Great when you want back stimulus without hinge fatigue.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Seated Cable Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The seated cable row is a horizontal pulling exercise that loads the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, trapezius, and elbow flexors under continuous cable tension. It is a foundational machine/cable row for back hypertrophy and pulling strength.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Biceps and other elbow flexors
- Erector spinae (isometric depending on torso angle)

### Stabilizers

- Core musculature
- Scapular stabilizers
- Hamstrings/hips if feet are braced

## Equipment

- Seated cable row station
- V-handle, straight bar, or rope
- Foot platform

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Sit tall with feet braced; hold the handle with arms extended and shoulders packed.
2. Pull the handle toward the torso by driving elbows back.
3. Retract the scapulae at the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4. Return under control to a stretch position without rounding excessively through the lumbar spine.
5. Keep the torso angle relatively stable (avoid large rock).

## Coaching Cues

- "Pull elbows back"
- "Chest tall"
- "Squeeze the shoulder blades"
- "Control the reach"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive torso rocking
- Shrugging traps
- Rounding the low back under load
- Cutting the stretch
- Using only arm curl motion

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Arms long with a loaded stretch to elbows-back peak contraction near the torso.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Pauses at contraction
- Single-arm cable row
- Chest-supported free-weight rows

## Regressions

- Chest-supported machine row
- Lighter load with stricter torso
- Inverted row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Primary horizontal-pull hypertrophy staple.

#### Strength

Builds general pulling strength.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep sets work well.

#### Fat Loss

Efficient back compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Barbell Shrug | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The barbell shrug isolates scapular elevation primarily for the upper trapezius. It is included in back programming for upper-back thickness and trap development, typically as a short accessory after heavier pulls.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Upper trapezius

### Secondary

- Levator scapulae
- Middle trapezius (stabilizing)

### Stabilizers

- Core bracing
- Grip musculature

## Equipment

- Barbell (dumbbell/trap-bar variations exist)
- Optional straps

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Stand tall holding a barbell at the thighs with arms long.
2. Elevate the scapulae straight up toward the ears without rolling.
3. Pause briefly at the top.
4. Lower under control to a full scapular depression stretch.
5. Keep elbows extended—do not turn it into an upright row.

## Coaching Cues

- "Up, not roll"
- "Arms long"
- "Pause at the top"
- "Full lower between reps"

## Common Mistakes

- Rolling the shoulders excessively
- Bending elbows into upright rows
- Using so much load that ROM disappears
- Neck craning

## Breathing

Exhale on the elevation; inhale on the lower.

## Range of Motion

Full scapular depression to full elevation without pain.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Longer pauses
- Dumbbell/trap-bar shrug variations

## Regressions

- Lighter shrugs
- Face-pull and upper-back rows for balanced development

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Upper-trap accessory hypertrophy.

#### Strength

Secondary; supports isometric holding strength for pulls.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep suitable.

#### Fat Loss

Optional low-skill accessory.

## Contraindications

Avoid aggressive loading with neck pain; use controlled ROM. Not medical advice.

Title: Single-Arm Cable Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The single-arm cable row is a unilateral horizontal pull that trains the lats and upper back while challenging anti-rotation core stability and allowing independent ROM per side.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-rotation musculature
- Scapular stabilizers
- Glutes/hips in staggered stance variations

## Equipment

- Single adjustable cable
- D-handle
- Optional bench or standing staggered stance

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Set cable around mid-torso height; stagger stance or sit supported.
2. Start arm long with shoulder packed.
3. Row the elbow back toward the hip/ribcage.
4. Squeeze the shoulder blade; return to stretch without twisting excessively.
5. Switch sides and match effort/ROM.

## Coaching Cues

- "Elbow to hip"
- "Square the torso"
- "Reach long, then row"
- "Do not rotate to cheat"

## Common Mistakes

- Rotating through the lumbar spine to move load
- Shrugging
- Short ROM
- Uneven sides

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full unilateral stretch to elbow-back contraction.

## Progressions

- Load
- Slow eccentrics
- Standing unsupported variations

## Regressions

- Seated bilateral cable row
- Chest-supported dumbbell row
- Machine single-arm row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets per side

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

High-quality unilateral back hypertrophy.

#### Strength

Helps address asymmetries.

#### Endurance

Higher reps suitable.

#### Fat Loss

Efficient accessory.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The single-arm lat pulldown is a unilateral vertical pull that allows independent loading, greater freedom of elbow path, and correction of side-to-side discrepancies in lat engagement.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Elbow flexors
- Rear deltoids
- Rhomboids

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-rotation musculature
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Single cable or unilateral pulldown handle
- Seat or kneeling stance
- Optional thigh support if using a standard station

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Grip a single handle overhead; stabilize the torso.
2. Pull the elbow down toward the ribcage until the hand reaches near the shoulder/chest line.
3. Emphasize lat contraction without excessive rotation.
4. Return to a full stretch overhead.
5. Complete all reps, then switch sides (or alternate).

## Coaching Cues

- "Elbow to back pocket"
- "Stretch tall"
- "Ribs down; do not twist wildly"
- "Match both sides"

## Common Mistakes

- Rotating the torso to move the stack
- Cutting the stretch
- Shrugging
- Unequal ROM between sides

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full unilateral overhead stretch to a strong side contraction.

## Progressions

- Load
- Slow eccentrics
- Kneeling single-arm pulldown with longer stretch

## Regressions

- Bilateral pulldown
- Assisted pull-up
- Straight-arm pulldown

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets per side

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds between sides/sets

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent unilateral lat hypertrophy tool.

#### Strength

Secondary; helps balance sides.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep friendly.

#### Fat Loss

Efficient accessory after bilateral pulls.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Smith Machine Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The Smith machine row is a rails-guided bent-over or upright-supported row variation. The fixed path can help some lifters overload horizontal pulling, but it constrains natural bar path and requires careful torso setup.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Spinal erectors (if hinged)

### Stabilizers

- Core hinge bracing
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Smith machine
- Optional bench for chest-supported Smith row setups
- Safety stops as needed

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set torso position (hinge or chest-supported) so the bar path meets the mid-torso.
2. Unhook; start arms long.
3. Row the bar to the torso; lower to stretch.
4. Keep spine neutral.
5. Re-hook securely after the set.

## Coaching Cues

- "Align the path to the torso"
- "Elbows back"
- "Neutral spine"
- "Re-hook fully"

## Common Mistakes

- Misaligned stance causing awkward shoulder angles
- Rounding under fatigue
- Bouncing off end stops
- Excessive upright shrug pattern

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Long-arm stretch to torso contact within a stable position.

## Progressions

- Load
- Pauses
- Free-weight row progressions

## Regressions

- Seated cable row
- Machine row
- Chest-supported dumbbell row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–150 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Guided overload option when free rows are limited.

#### Strength

Imperfect transfer to free barbell row.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Optional compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.
