Title: Standing Cable Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The standing cable row is a horizontal pull performed in a staggered or athletic stance, increasing core demand versus seated rows while loading the lats and upper back under continuous tension.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension/anti-rotation
- Hip/leg bracing in stance

## Equipment

- Adjustable cable at mid-torso height
- Handle or bar
- Clear space for stance

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set cable mid-height; take a staggered stance and brace.
2. Start arm(s) long with packed shoulders.
3. Row elbows back to the torso.
4. Return to stretch without losing the stance brace.
5. Keep ribs down—avoid turning into a hip hinge yank.

## Coaching Cues

- "Own the stance"
- "Elbows back"
- "Tall chest"
- "No torso flop"

## Common Mistakes

- Using hip drive as the prime mover
- Rounding under fatigue
- Partial stretch
- Stance too narrow

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Long-arm stretch to elbows-back finish.

## Progressions

- Load
- Single-arm standing row
- Slow eccentrics

## Regressions

- Seated cable row
- Chest-supported row
- Machine row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Horizontal pull with extra trunk demand.

#### Strength

Secondary.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep workable.

#### Fat Loss

Good when you want combined pull + brace work.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Straight-Arm Pulldown | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The straight-arm pulldown is a lat-isolation pattern performed with nearly extended elbows, emphasizing shoulder extension under cable tension. It is useful for teaching lat engagement and adding lengthened- or shortened-position lat work without heavy elbow-flexor fatigue.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Teres major
- Rear deltoids
- Triceps long head (as a shoulder extensor contributor)

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension
- Scapular depressors

## Equipment

- High cable
- Straight bar, lat bar, or rope

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Stand facing a high cable; grip the bar with arms nearly straight.
2. Hinge slightly; brace the trunk.
3. Sweep the bar down toward the thighs using shoulder extension (lats), keeping elbows softly locked.
4. Squeeze at the bottom; return under control to a stretch overhead/in front.
5. Avoid turning the movement into a triceps pushdown with heavy elbow bend.

## Coaching Cues

- "Soft elbows stay soft"
- "Push the bar to the thighs with the lats"
- "Ribs down"
- "Stretch up, squeeze down"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive elbow bend (becomes a pulldown/pushdown hybrid)
- Lumbar overarching
- Using momentum
- Shrugging

## Breathing

Exhale as the bar descends; inhale on the return stretch.

## Range of Motion

From a long overhead/front stretch to bar-near-thigh peak contraction.

## Progressions

- Load
- Slow eccentrics
- Single-arm straight-arm pulldown

## Regressions

- Lighter cable
- Machine pullover
- Band straight-arm pulldown

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

High-value lat isolation accessory.

#### Strength

Not a primary strength lift.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep suitable.

#### Fat Loss

Low-skill accessory after compounds.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: T-Bar Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The T-bar row is a hinged horizontal pull using a landmine/T-bar setup or dedicated T-bar station. It allows heavy loading of the lats and mid-back with a fixed bar path that many lifters find stable compared with a free barbell row.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Rhomboids and middle trapezius

### Secondary

- Rear deltoids
- Elbow flexors
- Spinal erectors (isometric)

### Stabilizers

- Core and hip hinge stabilizers
- Scapular retractors
- Grip musculature

## Equipment

- T-bar row station or barbell in landmine with handle attachment
- Weight plates
- Optional chest pad if machine provides one

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Straddle the bar; hinge to a stable torso angle with neutral spine.
2. Grip handles; start with arms long and shoulders packed.
3. Row by driving elbows back until the plates/handles approach the torso.
4. Squeeze the back; lower under control to a stretch.
5. Keep hips and torso angle relatively consistent—avoid standing upright each rep.

## Coaching Cues

- "Hinge and brace"
- "Elbows back"
- "Chest tall, not standing up"
- "Control the stretch"

## Common Mistakes

- Turning the set into a shrug-deadlift hybrid
- Rounding the lumbar spine
- Using plates that block ROM
- Yanking with hip extension every rep

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Long-arm stretch to elbows-back contraction without losing hinge posture.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Paused rows
- Chest-supported T-bar if available

## Regressions

- Chest-supported row
- Seated cable row
- Dumbbell row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Heavy mid-back and lat builder.

#### Strength

Strong overload row option.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Keep if hinge position stays crisp when fatigued.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Weighted Chin-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The weighted chin-up adds external load to the supinated-grip chin-up, allowing continued overload of the lats and elbow flexors after bodyweight chin-ups no longer provide sufficient stimulus.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi
- Elbow flexors (high contribution)

### Secondary

- Rhomboids and middle trapezius
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core
- Scapular stabilizers
- Grip musculature

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar
- Weight belt, vest, or dumbbell

## Difficulty

advanced

## Execution

1. Secure load; hang with a supinated grip.
2. Pull strictly until chin clears the bar.
3. Lower to a controlled dead hang.
4. Maintain shoulder packing under load.
5. Dismount and unload safely.

## Coaching Cues

- "Pack, then pull"
- "Elbows down and back"
- "No kip"
- "Control the negative"

## Common Mistakes

- Excess load causing incomplete ROM
- Elbow irritation ignored
- Swinging
- Unsafe belt setup

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Dead hang to chin-over-bar with control.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Pauses at the top
- Slow eccentrics

## Regressions

- Bodyweight chin-up
- Assisted chin-up
- Reverse-grip pulldown

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- 3–10

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 2–5 minutes

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Strong lat + biceps vertical-pull overload.

#### Strength

High-value pulling strength variation.

#### Endurance

Prefer lighter variations.

#### Fat Loss

Optional if elbows tolerate loading.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Monitor elbow flexor tendons closely.

Title: Weighted Pull-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The weighted pull-up adds external load (belt, vest, or dumbbell) to the standard pull-up to continue progressive overload after bodyweight repetitions become too easy for strength or hypertrophy goals.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Biceps and other elbow flexors
- Rhomboids and trapezius
- Rear deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core musculature
- Scapular depressors/retractors
- Grip musculature

## Equipment

- Pull-up bar
- Dip/pull-up belt with plates, weight vest, or carefully held dumbbell
- Optional chalk

## Difficulty

advanced

## Execution

1. Secure external load safely (belt preferred for heavy loading).
2. Perform a strict pull-up from dead hang to chin-over-bar.
3. Lower under control to full hang.
4. Maintain scapular packing under the added load.
5. Remove load safely after the set.

## Coaching Cues

- "Load secure before you pull"
- "Same strict standards as bodyweight"
- "Full hang, full chin clearance"
- "Control the eccentric"

## Common Mistakes

- Adding load before bodyweight technique is consistent
- Kipping to move heavier loads
- Incomplete ROM
- Unsafe load attachment

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full hang to chin-over-bar; prioritize ROM quality over load.

## Progressions

- Heavier external load
- Paused weighted reps
- Slow eccentrics
- Chest-to-bar weighted pull-ups

## Regressions

- Bodyweight pull-up
- Eccentric-only weighted or bodyweight negatives
- Lat pulldown heavy

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 3–6
- Hypertrophy: 5–10

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 2–5 minutes

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly for most due to systemic fatigue

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Primary tool to keep pull-ups progressive for muscle growth.

#### Strength

Excellent absolute pulling strength builder.

#### Endurance

Not first-line; use lighter bodyweight/assisted variations.

#### Fat Loss

Keep if recovery allows; reduce load before cutting ROM.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Wide-Grip Lat Pulldown | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The wide-grip lat pulldown uses a pronated grip wider than shoulder width on a pulldown bar to emphasize latissimus dorsi loading in a vertical pull pattern. It is a scalable alternative or accessory to wide-grip pull-ups.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Teres major
- Rear deltoids
- Biceps (less than closer grips for many lifters)

### Stabilizers

- Scapular retractors
- Core against the pad

## Equipment

- Lat pulldown station
- Long bar
- Thigh pad secured

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Secure thighs under the pad; grip the bar wide with a pronated grip.
2. Start with arms extended and a slight lean if preferred.
3. Pull the bar to the upper chest by driving elbows down.
4. Squeeze the back briefly; return under control to full stretch.
5. Avoid pulling behind the neck.

## Coaching Cues

- "Elbows down, not hands to chin only"
- "Bar to upper chest"
- "Control the stretch"
- "No behind-the-neck"

## Common Mistakes

- Behind-the-neck pulldowns
- Using too much momentum/lean
- Partial stretch at the top
- Excessive elbow flare without lat tension

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Full overhead stretch to upper-chest contact without painful shoulder positions.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Paused contractions
- Pull-up progressions

## Regressions

- Neutral-grip pulldown
- Assisted pull-up
- Single-arm pulldown lighter

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Staple vertical-pull hypertrophy variation.

#### Strength

Supports pull-up strength when overloaded progressively.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep sets work well.

#### Fat Loss

Efficient back compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Avoid behind-the-neck variations.

Accessory/compound hybrid.

Title: Yates Row | Category: exercise | Subcategory: back

## Overview

## Overview

The Yates row is an underhand (supinated) bent-over barbell row typically performed with a more upright torso angle than a near-parallel Pendlay-style row, emphasizing lat thickness and elbow-flexor involvement.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Latissimus dorsi

### Secondary

- Elbow flexors
- Rhomboids and trapezius
- Rear deltoids
- Spinal erectors (isometric)

### Stabilizers

- Core hinge bracing
- Grip
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Optional straps
- Clear platform

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Hinge to a moderate torso angle (often ~45° rather than fully parallel).
2. Take a supinated grip roughly shoulder-width.
3. Row the bar to the lower abdomen by driving elbows back.
4. Lower under control to a stretch without losing brace.
5. Keep the torso angle consistent.

## Coaching Cues

- "Underhand, elbows to hips"
- "Moderate hinge—not upright curling"
- "Brace the trunk"
- "Control the eccentric"

## Common Mistakes

- Becoming a reverse curl with no back engagement
- Rounding the lumbar spine
- Excessive upright torso turning it into a shrug
- Jerky reps

## Breathing

Inhale to prepare or during the eccentric lengthening phase. Exhale during the concentric pull (or near peak contraction). Brace the trunk; avoid breath-holding that causes dizziness on high-rep sets.

## Range of Motion

Arms long to bar-to-abdomen contraction within a stable hinge.

## Progressions

- Load
- Pause reps
- Stricter torso angles

## Regressions

- Reverse-grip seated cable row
- Chest-supported underhand machine row
- Dumbbell row

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Lat-biased free-weight row with strong elbow-flexor contribution.

#### Strength

Secondary row strength.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Optional if elbows tolerate underhand loading.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic shoulder impingement, acute elbow tendinopathy, recent lat or biceps strain, uncontrolled low-back pain during hinged positions, or inability to control scapular motion. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis. Supinated gripping may aggravate elbow flexor tendons.

Title: Barbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

The barbell bench press is a horizontal pressing exercise that loads the pectoralis major with substantial contribution from the triceps brachii and anterior deltoids. It is widely used for upper-body strength and hypertrophy because it allows progressive overload with measurable load increments and has extensive support in resistance-training research and professional guidelines.

## Primary Muscles

- Pectoralis major (sternal and clavicular heads)

## Secondary Muscles

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids
- Serratus anterior (stabilization)
- Scapular retractors (stabilization)

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Flat bench
- Power rack or dedicated bench press station
- Safety pins or spotter recommended for near-maximal loads

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Benefits

- Efficient compound stimulus for chest, triceps, and front delts
- High capacity for progressive overload and strength tracking
- Strong transfer to horizontal pressing performance
- Well studied in hypertrophy and strength literature as a primary free-weight press

## Execution

1. Lie on a flat bench with eyes roughly under the bar. Plant feet firmly. Retract and depress the scapulae; maintain a stable upper-back position.
2. Grip the bar evenly (commonly slightly wider than shoulder width). Unrack with locked elbows and bring the bar over the mid-chest/shoulder line.
3. Lower the bar under control to the mid-to-lower chest while elbows track at a moderate angle (typically ~45–70° from the torso, individualized to shoulder comfort).
4. Press the bar upward and slightly back toward the start position until elbows are extended without losing scapular stability.
5. Re-rack only when the bar is stable over the supports.

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive elbow flare that increases anterior shoulder stress
- Bouncing the bar off the chest and losing eccentric control
- Losing scapular retraction and turning the press into a shoulder-dominant pattern
- Uncontrolled arch that lifts the hips off the bench
- Incomplete range that chronically shortens the pressing ROM without a programming reason

## Coaching Cues

- “Pins back and down; chest up”
- “Break the bar and lower to the chest”
- “Drive feet into the floor as you press”
- “Finish over the shoulders, not over the face”

## Programming

Use as a primary horizontal press on upper or push days. For strength, prioritize lower-rep heavy sets with longer rests. For hypertrophy, use moderate loads with controlled eccentrics and proximity to failure managed via RIR. Pair with incline pressing or fly/cable work when greater clavicular-chest or stretch-biased volume is desired.

Title: Barbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Sets

- Strength focus: 3–5 sets
- Hypertrophy focus: 3–4 sets

## Reps

- Strength focus: 3–6 reps
- Hypertrophy focus: 6–12 reps

## Tempo

- Hypertrophy: 2-0-1-0 to 3-1-1-0
- Strength: controlled eccentric, intentional concentric (often 2-0-X-0)

## Rest Time

- Strength focus: 2–5 minutes
- Hypertrophy focus: 90–180 seconds

## Variations

- Pause bench press
- Close-grip bench press
- Incline barbell bench press
- Dumbbell bench press

## Regression

- Dumbbell bench press
- Machine chest press
- Push-up

## Progression

- Paused heavy singles/doubles
- Tempo eccentrics
- Competition-style pause bench
- Progressive overload via load, reps, or set volume

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent pectoralis or triceps strain, uncontrolled wrist/elbow pain, or when a safe rack/spotting setup is unavailable. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Science Summary

Horizontal pressing is a core pattern in resistance-training recommendations for upper-body strength and muscle development. EMG and training studies consistently show high pectoralis major involvement in the flat bench press, with meaningful triceps and anterior deltoid contribution. Hypertrophy outcomes depend more on sufficient weekly volume, progressive overload, and proximity to failure than on any single exercise, but the bench press remains an effective primary loader because external resistance can be progressed precisely. Grip width and elbow angle alter joint stress and regional emphasis; individual anthropometry should guide technique within a controlled ROM.

Title: Cable Chest Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The cable chest press is a standing or seated horizontal press using dual cables, providing continuous tension and a customizable path for pectoralis major loading with elevated core demand when standing.

- Handles

intermediate

1. Set cables near mid-chest; hold handles at the sides of the chest and step forward into a split stance.

3. Press handles forward to extension without shrugging.
4. Return under control to the chest.

Exhale on press; inhale on return.

Title: Cable Fly | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The cable fly (often a mid-height standing cable crossover/fly) isolates the pectoralis major through humeral adduction under continuous tension. Unlike dumbbell flies, cables maintain resistance near peak contraction, which is useful for hypertrophy accessories.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids
- Biceps brachii (minor stabilizing role)

### Stabilizers

- Core and scapular musculature in standing variations
- Rotator cuff for humeral control

## Equipment

- Dual cable station
- Handles
- Optional staggered stance for balance

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set cables around mid-chest height. Grab handles and step forward into tension.
2. Start arms open with a slight elbow bend and soft scapular set.
3. Bring handles together in an arc via shoulder horizontal adduction.
4. Squeeze briefly at peak contraction without shrugging.
5. Return under control to a stretch without painful end-range positions.

## Coaching Cues

- "Soft elbows, fixed angle"
- "Hug a barrel"
- "Squeeze at the midline"
- "Control the stretch on the way out"

## Common Mistakes

- Turning the fly into a press
- Torso swing/momentum
- Overstretching into pain
- Shrugging traps
- Asymmetric heights or stance

## Breathing

Exhale as handles meet; inhale as arms open. Brace to avoid lumbar sway.

## Range of Motion

Open to a challenging comfortable stretch; close until hands meet or cross slightly based on shoulder comfort.

## Progressions

- Increase load
- Slow eccentrics
- Peak-contraction pauses
- Single-arm cable fly

## Regressions

- Pec deck
- Light dumbbell fly
- Supported machine fly

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15 (hypertrophy default)

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3; prioritize tension over load

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 times weekly as accessory volume

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent isolation finisher with continuous tension.

#### Strength

Not a primary strength builder.

#### Endurance

Works well for higher-rep metabolic sets.

#### Fat Loss

Useful accessory after compound presses.

## Contraindications

Avoid deep stretch positions that provoke shoulder pain; reduce ROM or use supported machine fly. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Chest Dip | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The chest dip is a parallel-bar press performed with a slight forward torso lean to bias the pectoralis major relative to a more upright triceps-dominant dip. It is a high-tension compound movement for intermediate+ trainees when shoulder comfort allows.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular depressors and retractors
- Core musculature
- Rotator cuff

## Equipment

- Parallel bars or dip station
- Optional assistance band or machine
- Optional weight belt for progression

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Support on parallel bars with elbows extended and shoulders depressed.
2. Lean slightly forward and descend by bending the elbows.
3. Lower until upper arms are near parallel or to a pain-free depth.
4. Press to full extension while maintaining the forward lean bias.
5. Keep the descent controlled; avoid bouncing.

## Coaching Cues

- "Slight lean for chest bias"
- "Shoulders packed down"
- "Chest between the bars"
- "Press the bars away"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive depth causing anterior shoulder pain
- Too-upright torso when chest bias is intended
- Kipping/swinging
- Shrugging
- Uncontrolled flare under fatigue

## Breathing

Inhale on the descent; exhale on the press.

## Range of Motion

Parallel upper-arm depth is a common target; deeper only if controlled and pain-free.

## Progressions

- Weighted dips
- Slower eccentrics
- Ring dips (advanced)

## Regressions

- Band-assisted dips
- Machine-assisted dips
- Push-up variations

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- Bodyweight hypertrophy: 6–12
- Weighted strength-biased: 4–8

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3; start conservative on depth

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2 times weekly for most lifters due to joint stress

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent compound chest/triceps builder when tolerated.

#### Strength

Strong relative-strength and weighted progression tool.

#### Endurance

Higher reps possible with assistance.

#### Fat Loss

Keep if recovered; otherwise substitute machine press.

## Contraindications

Often poorly tolerated with anterior shoulder irritation, AC joint pain, or inadequate scapular control. Reduce depth or choose another press. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Decline Barbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The decline barbell bench press uses a declined torso position, often increasing relative emphasis on the sternal (lower) pectoralis fibers while reducing some shoulder flexion demand versus steep incline work. It is a compound press for hypertrophy and strength accessory programming when setup is secure.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major (sternal/lower fibers often relatively emphasized)

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular retractors
- Trunk musculature secured by decline pads

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Decline bench with secure leg supports
- Rack or partner hand-off when needed

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Secure legs under the decline pads and set a stable upper-back position.
2. Take an even grip; unrack carefully (partner hand-off is often safer).
3. Hold the bar over the lower-to-mid chest line.
4. Lower under control to the chest with wrists stacked over elbows.
5. Press to lockout and re-rack with assistance if required.

## Coaching Cues

- "Secure the legs before unracking"
- "Lower to the lower chest"
- "Control the eccentric; do not bounce"
- "Press evenly to lockout"

## Common Mistakes

- Unstable leg securement
- Excessive bounce
- Aggressive elbow flare
- Unsafe unracking/racking
- Extreme decline creating instability

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

Touch or approach the lower/mid chest with a controlled path. Do not sacrifice shoulder comfort for extreme depth.

## Progressions

- Progressive overload
- Pause reps
- Tempo eccentrics

## Regressions

- Decline dumbbell press
- Flat dumbbell press
- Machine chest press
- Assisted chest dip

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- Hypertrophy: 6–12
- Strength accessory: 4–8

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3 for most working sets

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds (up to 3 minutes for heavy sets)

### Frequency

- 1–2 sessions weekly as part of total press volume

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Useful for lower-chest emphasis within a balanced pressing menu.

#### Strength

Accessory for most lifters; flat bench remains primary for powerlifting specificity.

#### Endurance

Prefer push-ups or machine press for high-rep endurance work.

#### Fat Loss

Keep if technique and secure setup remain safe when fatigued.

## Contraindications

Avoid if decline positioning causes dizziness, uncontrolled shoulder pain, or if the bench cannot be secured safely. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Decline Dumbbell Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The decline dumbbell press loads the pectoralis major on a declined bench with independent dumbbells, often emphasizing sternal fibers while allowing a natural shoulder path and deep stretch.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major (sternal emphasis often increased)

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular retractors
- Rotator cuff

## Equipment

- Dumbbells
- Decline bench with secure leg supports

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Secure legs; bring dumbbells to the start position at the sides of the chest.
2. Press to elbow extension without clanging aggressively.
3. Lower under control into a stretch.
4. Maintain even depth and tempo.
5. Sit up carefully after the set.

## Coaching Cues

- "Secure legs first"
- "Lower into a controlled stretch"
- "Wrists over elbows"
- "Even lockout"

## Common Mistakes

- Insecure leg position
- Excessive bounce
- Asymmetrical ROM
- Unsafe teardown

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

Full comfortable stretch and lockout; avoid painful shoulder end ranges.

## Progressions

- Heavier loads
- Tempo eccentrics
- Pauses

## Regressions

- Machine press
- Flat dumbbell press
- Assisted dips

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–150 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Useful lower-chest biased free-weight press.

#### Strength

Accessory only.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Optional compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent pectoralis or triceps strain, uncontrolled wrist/elbow pain, or when a safe setup/spot cannot be arranged. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Deficit Push-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The deficit push-up elevates the hands so the chest can descend below hand level. Increased ROM provides a larger stretch stimulus to the pectoralis major while retaining closed-chain push-up mechanics.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Serratus anterior
- Trunk musculature in plank position

## Equipment

- Bodyweight
- Parallettes, sturdy handles, or stable equal-height plates

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Place hands on equal-height elevated surfaces near shoulder width.
2. Assume a rigid plank.
3. Lower the chest below hand level through a controlled stretch.
4. Press to full elbow extension.
5. Maintain alignment; do not sag to buy depth.

## Coaching Cues

- "Chest below the hands"
- "Plank stays tight"
- "Soft stretch, not a dump into the shoulders"
- "Push the handles away"

## Common Mistakes

- Deficit too large for comfort
- Hip sagging
- Unstable hand surfaces
- Uncontrolled elbow flare
- Bouncing out of the bottom

## Breathing

Inhale into the bottom stretch; exhale on the ascent.

## Range of Motion

Deep but pain-free stretch. Reduce deficit height if shoulders complain.

## Progressions

- Greater deficit (gradual)
- Weighted vest
- Slow eccentrics / stretch pauses
- Ring push-up

## Regressions

- Standard push-up
- Incline push-up
- Smaller deficit

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds (up to 150 s if weighted)

### Frequency

- 1–3 times weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Strong bodyweight option emphasizing stretch-mediated stimulus.

#### Strength

Good relative-strength builder when loaded.

#### Endurance

Use moderate deficits for higher reps.

#### Fat Loss

Effective when standard push-up capacity is already solid.

## Contraindications

Avoid large deficits with anterior shoulder pain or poor scapular control at depth. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Dumbbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The dumbbell bench press is a flat-bench horizontal press using independent dumbbells. It loads the pectoralis major, triceps, and anterior deltoids while allowing a natural wrist/shoulder path and, for many lifters, a deeper stretch ROM than a barbell.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Serratus anterior
- Rotator cuff (dynamic stability)
- Scapular retractors

## Equipment

- Pair of dumbbells
- Flat bench

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Sit with dumbbells on thighs; lie back while bringing the dumbbells to the sides of the chest.
2. Plant feet; lightly retract scapulae against the bench.
3. Press until elbows extend; avoid forcefully clanging the bells.
4. Lower under control to a deep but comfortable stretch near chest level.
5. After the set, return dumbbells to the thighs and sit up safely.

## Coaching Cues

- "Wrists stacked over elbows"
- "Lower into a controlled stretch"
- "Press up without losing back contact"
- "Soft lockout, not a crash together"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive elbow flare
- Chronically short ROM
- Hips lifting off the bench
- Unsafe setup/teardown
- Dumbbells drifting forward of the shoulder line

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

Seek a full stretch at the bottom without painful anterior shoulder positions. Prioritize left-right symmetry.

## Progressions

- Heavier dumbbells
- Slow eccentrics
- Pauses in the stretch
- Single-arm dumbbell bench press

## Regressions

- Machine chest press
- Floor press
- Push-up
- Neutral-grip dumbbell press with lighter load

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- Hypertrophy: 8–12
- Strength-biased: 5–8

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 times per week within weekly pressing volume

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Excellent primary or secondary flat press due to ROM and independent loading.

#### Strength

Strong accessory; load jumps are less precise than small barbell plates.

#### Endurance

Higher reps are feasible with lighter dumbbells.

#### Fat Loss

Retain as a compound lift; reduce sets before sacrificing technique.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent pectoralis or triceps strain, uncontrolled wrist/elbow pain, or when a safe setup/spot cannot be arranged. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Dumbbell Fly | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The dumbbell fly is an isolation exercise emphasizing pectoralis major lengthening and adduction on a flat bench. Resistance is highest near the stretch and decreases toward the top, so control and moderate loads matter more than heavy loading.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Rotator cuff
- Scapular retractors against the bench

## Equipment

- Light-to-moderate dumbbells
- Flat bench

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells over the chest with soft elbows.
2. Open the arms in a wide arc until a deep comfortable stretch is reached.
3. Keep elbow angle relatively fixed.
4. Reverse the arc by adducting until dumbbells return over the chest.
5. Avoid turning the movement into a press.

## Coaching Cues

- "Hug a wide barrel"
- "Soft elbows stay soft"
- "Stretch under control"
- "Do not press the weight up"

## Common Mistakes

- Excessive load forcing a press pattern
- Dangerous overstretch
- Bent elbows changing every rep
- Bouncing out of the bottom

## Breathing

Inhale into the stretch; exhale as arms return.

## Range of Motion

Deep stretch without anterior shoulder pain; finish over mid-chest.

## Progressions

- Slightly heavier loads with control
- Slow eccentrics
- Incline dumbbell fly
- Cable fly for continuous tension

## Regressions

- Pec deck
- Cable fly light
- Shorter ROM fly

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- RIR 2–3 (leave technique buffer)

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Classic stretch-biased chest isolation.

#### Strength

Not for strength.

#### Endurance

Light higher-rep sets possible.

#### Fat Loss

Accessory only.

## Contraindications

Avoid aggressive end-range stretches with shoulder irritation. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Overview

Title: Floor Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The floor press is a horizontal press performed lying on the floor, which shortens ROM by stopping when the triceps meet the floor. It reduces shoulder extension demand and emphasizes mid-range pressing strength for the chest and triceps.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular retractors
- Trunk against the floor

## Equipment

- Barbell or dumbbells
- Flat floor space
- Optional rack for barbell floor press

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Lie on the floor under the bar (or with dumbbells). Plant feet or extend legs based on preference.
2. Unrack and hold over the chest.
3. Lower until upper arms lightly contact the floor.
4. Pause briefly to eliminate bounce.
5. Press to lockout.

## Coaching Cues

- "Touch the floor softly with the arms"
- "Pause, then press"
- "Keep upper back tight"
- "No bounce off the floor"

## Common Mistakes

- Bouncing elbows off the floor
- Excessive flare
- Losing bar path over the chest
- Rushing the pause

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

From lockout down to upper-arm floor contact; intentionally partial versus full bench ROM.

## Progressions

- Heavier paused reps
- Close-grip floor press
- Transition to full ROM bench

## Regressions

- Machine press
- Push-up
- Lighter dumbbell floor press

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 3–6
- Hypertrophy: 6–10

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 2–4 minutes for heavy work

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Useful overload with less shoulder stress for some lifters.

#### Strength

Excellent mid-range lockout strength builder.

#### Endurance

Not first-line.

#### Fat Loss

Optional compound.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent pectoralis or triceps strain, uncontrolled wrist/elbow pain, or when a safe setup/spot cannot be arranged. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: High Cable Fly | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The high cable fly uses high pulleys and a high-to-low arc, often increasing relative emphasis on the sternal/lower pectoralis fibers while maintaining continuous cable tension through adduction.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major (sternal/lower fibers relatively emphasized)

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids
- Serratus anterior (depending on scapular motion)

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension/anti-rotation musculature
- Rotator cuff

## Equipment

- Dual high cable pulleys
- Handles

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set both pulleys high; grasp handles and step forward to create tension.
2. Start with arms elevated and open, elbows softly bent.
3. Sweep handles downward and inward toward the lower chest/upper abdomen line.
4. Pause briefly with the pectoralis major contracted.
5. Return slowly without changing elbow angle.

## Coaching Cues

- "High to low"
- "Lead with the elbows in an arc"
- "Finish low at the midline"
- "No torso fold"

## Common Mistakes

- Triceps pushdown pattern
- Excessive trunk flexion
- Locked/strained elbows
- Overstretching at the top
- Jerky return

## Breathing

Exhale on the downward squeeze; inhale on the return.

## Range of Motion

Smooth arc from a comfortable overhead-open position to a low midline finish; stop if the shoulder feels pinched.

## Progressions

- Load, tempo, or peak pause
- Single-arm high-to-low fly

## Regressions

- Mid cable fly
- Pec deck
- Decline-oriented press accessories

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 times weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Accessory for lower-chest emphasis and continuous tension.

#### Strength

Not primary.

#### Endurance

Suitable for higher reps.

#### Fat Loss

Accessory after compounds.

## Contraindications

Reduce ROM or avoid if overhead-open positions irritate the shoulder. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Incline Barbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

The incline barbell bench press is performed on an inclined bench and loads the pectoralis major with increased relative demand on the clavicular fibers and anterior deltoids compared with flat pressing. A moderate incline preserves a pressing pattern while allowing precise barbell progressive overload.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major (greater relative clavicular-head emphasis at moderate inclines)

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids
- Triceps brachii

### Stabilizers

- Serratus anterior
- Scapular retractors
- Trunk musculature against the bench

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Incline bench (commonly ~15–45°)
- Rack or dedicated incline station
- Spotter or safety arms recommended for heavy sets

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set a moderate incline (often 15–45°). Lie with feet planted and eyes roughly under the bar.
2. Retract and depress the scapulae; grip evenly, slightly wider than shoulder width.
3. Unrack and hold the bar over the upper chest/shoulder line.
4. Lower under control to the upper-chest contact point with elbows at a moderate, comfortable angle.
5. Press to full elbow extension without losing upper-back contact, then re-rack when stable.

## Coaching Cues

- "Moderate incline, not a shoulder press"
- "Upper back tight; chest up"
- "Lower to the upper chest"
- "Drive evenly through both arms"

## Common Mistakes

- Incline set too steep (becomes a shoulder press)
- Excessive elbow flare
- Bouncing the bar
- Losing scapular support and shrugging
- Uneven bar path

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

Use full controllable ROM to the upper chest without painful shoulder positions. Avoid chronically shortened ROM unless specifically programmed.

## Progressions

- Heavier load with solid technique
- Paused incline reps
- Slow eccentrics (3–4 s)
- Lower RIR over a mesocycle

## Regressions

- Incline dumbbell press
- Incline machine chest press
- Landmine press
- Elevated-hand push-up

## Programming

### Sets

- Strength: 3–5 sets
- Hypertrophy: 3–4 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 3–6
- Hypertrophy: 6–12

### Intensity

- Strength: ~80–90% 1RM or RIR 1–3
- Hypertrophy: ~65–80% 1RM or RIR 1–3

### Rest

- Strength: 2–5 minutes
- Hypertrophy: 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 sessions per week within total chest/push volume

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Primary or secondary upper-chest press; pair with flat pressing and fly/cable work.

#### Strength

Useful incline strength accessory; flat bench remains more specific for competition pressing.

#### Endurance

Higher-rep sets (12–20) with lighter loads if conditioning is the goal.

#### Fat Loss

Keep as a compound lift in a deficit; manage volume to protect recovery.

Title: Incline Dumbbell Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

The incline dumbbell press is an upper-horizontal pressing variation performed on an inclined bench. Compared with flat pressing, a moderate incline increases relative demand on the clavicular fibers of the pectoralis major and the anterior deltoids while still loading the triceps. Independent dumbbells also allow a more natural wrist/shoulder path and a deeper stretch position for many lifters.

## Primary Muscles

- Pectoralis major (greater relative clavicular-head emphasis at moderate inclines)

## Secondary Muscles

- Anterior deltoids
- Triceps brachii
- Serratus anterior (stabilization)

## Equipment

- Pair of dumbbells
- Adjustable bench set to a moderate incline (commonly ~15–45°)

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Benefits

- Useful for upper-chest hypertrophy when added to flat pressing volume
- Allows independent limb loading and easier joint-friendly pathing than a fixed barbell
- Supports a large ROM and stretch-biased stimulus at the bottom position
- Simple to progress with small dumbbell increments or added reps

## Execution

1. Set the bench to a moderate incline. Sit, then kick or hoist the dumbbells to the start position at shoulder level.
2. Retract the scapulae lightly against the bench. Keep feet planted and ribs down.
3. Press the dumbbells upward until elbows are extended without forcefully slamming the bells together.
4. Lower under control until the elbows reach a challenging but comfortable depth, typically near chest level, while maintaining shoulder stability.
5. Repeat for the target reps; bring the dumbbells down safely to the thighs before standing.

## Common Mistakes

- Setting the incline too steep and converting the movement into a near-shoulder press
- Flaring elbows aggressively and losing scapular support
- Shortening the eccentric and removing the stretch stimulus
- Arching through the lumbar spine instead of bracing against the bench
- Letting dumbbells drift forward of the shoulder line

## Coaching Cues

- “Moderate incline, not a shoulder press”
- “Lower with control into the stretch”
- “Wrists stacked over elbows”
- “Press up without losing upper-back contact”

## Programming

Best used as a primary or secondary hypertrophy press on push/upper days. Pair with a flat press or push-up variation for balanced chest development. Prefer moderate loads that allow full control through the bottom ROM. If shoulders feel irritated, reduce incline, narrow ROM slightly, or substitute a machine incline press.

## Sets

- 3–4 sets

## Reps

- 8–12 reps (hypertrophy default)
- 6–8 reps when using heavier dumbbells with solid control

Title: Incline Dumbbell Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Tempo

- 2-0-1-0 to 3-1-1-0

## Rest Time

- 90–180 seconds

## Variations

- Incline barbell press
- Neutral-grip incline dumbbell press
- Incline machine press
- Single-arm incline dumbbell press

## Regression

- Incline machine press
- Landmine press
- Elevated push-up (hands on bench)

## Progression

- Heavier dumbbells
- Deeper controlled ROM
- Slow eccentric emphasis
- Added sets within recoverable weekly chest volume

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with symptomatic anterior shoulder pain, recent pectoralis strain, or inability to safely get dumbbells into position. Very steep inclines may aggravate shoulders in some lifters. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Science Summary

Research comparing bench angles shows that incline pressing increases relative clavicular pectoralis and anterior deltoid involvement versus flat pressing, while flat pressing often remains highly effective for sternal pectoralis loading. Dumbbell pressing can produce similar or favorable pectoralis activation with greater freedom of movement than a barbell for many trainees. Hypertrophy still depends on progressive tension and weekly volume; incline dumbbell work is best treated as a complementary press that expands stimulus variety and ROM rather than a mandatory replacement for flat pressing.

B

Title: Pause Barbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The pause barbell bench press inserts a deliberate pause on the chest, removing stretch-reflex contribution and increasing control demands. It is a strength and hypertrophy variation of the flat barbell bench press used to improve technique and pressing power off the chest.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular retractors
- Trunk and leg drive musculature

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Flat bench and rack
- Spotter/safeties recommended

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Set up as in the barbell bench press.
2. Lower under control to the chest.
3. Pause motionless on the chest for the prescribed time (commonly 1 second).
4. Press explosively to lockout without losing positions.
5. Re-rack safely.

## Coaching Cues

- "Settle on the chest, still"
- "No bounce"
- "Drive after the pause"
- "Keep upper back tight during the pause"

## Common Mistakes

- Soft bounce disguised as a pause
- Losing tightness during the pause
- Flaring under fatigue
- Inconsistent pause lengths

## Breathing

Inhale on descent/brace; brief hold during pause if appropriate; exhale on press.

## Range of Motion

Full touch with a true motionless pause; lockout each rep.

## Progressions

- Longer pauses
- Heavier paused work
- Chains/bands only if already proficient

## Regressions

- Touch-and-go bench with lighter load
- Floor press
- Dumbbell press

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–5 sets

### Reps

- Strength: 2–5
- Hypertrophy: 5–8

### Intensity

- Often slightly below touch-and-go loads; RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 2–5 minutes

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Improves control and time under tension off the chest.

#### Strength

Highly specific for paused pressing strength.

#### Endurance

Not ideal.

#### Fat Loss

Use lighter paused technique work if fatigued.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent pectoralis or triceps strain, uncontrolled wrist/elbow pain, or when a safe setup/spot cannot be arranged. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Pec Deck | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The pec deck (machine fly) isolates the pectoralis major on a fixed arc with back support. Reduced cheating via torso momentum makes it accessible for controlled hypertrophy work.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Minimal versus standing cables; scapular positioning against the pad still matters

## Equipment

- Pec deck / machine fly
- Adjustable seat and arm pads or handles

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Set seat height so elbows/forearms align near mid-chest.
2. Place forearms on pads (or grip handles) with a soft elbow bend.
3. Bring arms together through horizontal adduction toward midline.
4. Squeeze briefly; return under control to a comfortable stretch.
5. Avoid slamming the stack.

## Coaching Cues

- "Seat height so elbows are level"
- "Hug inward, do not press"
- "Control the opening stretch"
- "Ribs down on the pad"

## Common Mistakes

- Seat height causing impingement angles
- Pressing instead of flying
- Bouncing out of the stretch with excessive load
- Neck jutting forward
- Uncontrolled eccentrics

## Breathing

Exhale as arms close; inhale as arms open.

## Range of Motion

Open only within a pain-free stretch; close to near full adduction.

## Progressions

- Load increases
- Tempo eccentrics
- Peak-contraction pauses

## Regressions

- Lighter load
- Partial pain-free arc
- Light cable fly

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 times weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Reliable isolation volume with easy progressive overload.

#### Strength

Not a strength priority lift.

#### Endurance

Effective for higher-rep sets.

#### Fat Loss

Optional accessory after presses.

## Contraindications

Stop deep stretch if it causes sharp shoulder pain; adjust seat or choose cables. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Push-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

The push-up is a closed-chain horizontal pressing exercise that loads the pectoralis major, triceps, and anterior deltoids while requiring trunk stability. It is scalable from wall or knee variations to advanced loaded or deficit versions, making it suitable for beginners and as accessory or home-training work for trained individuals.

## Primary Muscles

- Pectoralis major

## Secondary Muscles

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids
- Serratus anterior
- Abdominals and other trunk stabilizers

## Equipment

- Bodyweight
- Optional: parallettes, handles, weight vest, or elevated surfaces for regressions/progressions

## Difficulty

beginner

## Benefits

- Accessible horizontal press with minimal equipment
- Trains pressing strength and hypertrophy potential when progressed sufficiently
- Concurrent trunk stability demand compared with supported bench pressing
- Easy to modify difficulty via leverage, ROM, tempo, or external load

## Execution

1. Place hands roughly under or slightly outside the shoulders. Extend the body into a plank: ribs down, glutes lightly engaged, head neutral.
2. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows while maintaining a rigid trunk.
3. Descend until the chest approaches the floor or reaches the deepest controllable ROM without losing plank alignment.
4. Press through the hands to full elbow extension while keeping scapulae moving naturally (avoid collapsing or extreme winging).
5. Reset tension and repeat.

## Common Mistakes

- Sagging hips or piking the pelvis, reducing transfer to the chest press pattern
- Cutting depth chronically without progression intent
- Flaring elbows hard to 90° and irritating the shoulders
- Leading with the head or cervical hyperextension
- Losing scapular control and dumping into the shoulders at the bottom

## Coaching Cues

- “Body in one line from head to heels”
- “Screw hands into the floor”
- “Chest to the floor, not hips first”
- “Push the floor away”

## Programming

Use as a primary press for beginners/home trainees or as accessory volume after heavier bench work. For hypertrophy, train near technical failure with progressions that keep reps in a productive range (roughly 6–15+ depending on variation). Increase difficulty before chasing very high-rep sets that become trunk-limited or form-limited.

## Sets

- 2–4 sets

## Reps

- Beginners: 5–12 controlled reps per set (use regressions as needed)
- Intermediate+: 6–15 reps on a challenging variation

## Tempo

- 2-0-1-0 to 3-1-1-0

## Rest Time

- 60–120 seconds
- Up to 180 seconds for hard weighted or deficit variations

Title: Push-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Variations

- Knee push-up
- Elevated-hand push-up
- Deficit push-up
- Tempo push-up
- Weighted vest push-up
- Diamond or close-grip push-up

## Regression

- Wall push-up
- Incline push-up (hands elevated)
- Knee push-up

## Progression

- Deficit push-up
- Feet-elevated push-up
- Weighted push-up
- Paused or slow-eccentric push-up
- Ring or unstable-surface push-up (advanced stability demand)

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate with acute wrist pain, symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent chest/shoulder strain, or inability to maintain plank alignment without pain. Modify hand elevation or use handles if wrist extension is poorly tolerated. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Science Summary

Push-ups produce substantial pectoralis major and triceps activation and can improve upper-body strength and muscle thickness when loading is progressed. Comparative work shows that sufficiently hard push-up variations can approximate aspects of bench-press muscle recruitment, though absolute external load and overload precision remain higher with free weights. Because bodyweight difficulty is leverage-dependent, programming should prioritize harder variations or added load once high-rep sets no longer provide progressive stimulus. Core involvement is higher than in bench pressing due to the unsupported plank position.

A

Title: Resistance Band Chest Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The resistance band chest press is a portable horizontal press using elastic resistance. Accommodating resistance increases load toward lockout and provides a home-training or warm-up option for the pectoralis major, triceps, and anterior deltoids.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-extension musculature in standing variations
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Resistance band(s)
- Stable anchor at mid-chest height (or band around the back for press-outs)
- Handles optional

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Anchor the band at roughly mid-chest height, or loop a band around the upper back for press-outs.
2. Hold handles at the sides of the chest; step out to create tension.
3. Press forward to extension without shrugging.
4. Return under control, keeping tension on the band.
5. Match left/right press paths.

## Coaching Cues

- "Create tension before the first press"
- "Press through mid-chest line"
- "Control the return"
- "Do not let the band snap you back"

## Common Mistakes

- Slack at the start of the rep
- Excessive lumbar extension
- Uneven arm paths
- Anchor failure / unsafe setup

## Breathing

Exhale on press; inhale on return.

## Range of Motion

From chest-level start to near-full elbow extension with continuous band tension.

## Progressions

- Heavier/thicker bands
- Slow eccentrics
- Single-arm band press
- Transition to dumbbell/cable press

## Regressions

- Lighter band
- Wall push-up
- Incline push-up

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 10–20

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 45–90 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Convenient hypertrophy stimulus when gym equipment is limited.

#### Strength

Limited maximal strength overload versus free weights.

#### Endurance

Excellent higher-rep option.

#### Fat Loss

Useful minimal-equipment compound.

## Contraindications

Ensure anchors are secure. Stop if shoulder pain appears. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Reverse-Grip Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The reverse-grip bench press uses a supinated grip on the barbell, which can increase upper-chest and triceps emphasis for some lifters. It requires careful setup and lower loads than a pronated bench due to grip security and unfamiliar groove.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major (clavicular fibers may be relatively emphasized)

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Forearm flexors for grip
- Scapular retractors

## Equipment

- Barbell
- Flat bench and rack
- Spotter strongly recommended
- Optional thumb wraps / secure grip practices

## Difficulty

advanced

## Execution

1. Set up as in a flat bench press but take a supinated (reverse) grip with thumbs around the bar.
2. Unrack carefully with a spotter when possible.
3. Lower under control to the chest with elbows tracking appropriately.
4. Press to lockout without losing grip security.
5. Re-rack with assistance.

## Coaching Cues

- "Thumbs around the bar"
- "Spotter for unrack and rack"
- "Controlled groove"
- "Do not chase pronated bench loads"

## Common Mistakes

- Thumbless grip (high risk)
- Excessive load early
- No spotter on heavy attempts
- Elbow positions that stress wrists/shoulders

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

Full controllable touch and press; prioritize grip security over depth ego.

## Progressions

- Gradual load increases only after groove mastery
- Pause reps light

## Regressions

- Incline dumbbell press
- Close-grip push-up
- Standard barbell bench

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–10

### Intensity

- Conservative RIR 2–4 until proficient

### Rest

- 2–3 minutes

### Frequency

- 1x weekly for most

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Optional variety for upper-chest/triceps emphasis.

#### Strength

Not first-line for most strength goals.

#### Endurance

Poor choice due to grip risk when fatigued.

#### Fat Loss

Prefer safer presses when fatigued.

## Contraindications

High technical/grip risk. Avoid with wrist issues or without a spotter. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Ring Push-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The ring push-up is an unstable closed-chain horizontal press on gymnastic rings. Instability increases demand on the chest, triceps, anterior deltoids, serratus, and trunk versus floor push-ups, making it an advanced progression when volume is controlled.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids
- Serratus anterior

### Stabilizers

- Rotator cuff
- Abdominals and trunk musculature
- Scapular stabilizers

## Equipment

- Gymnastic rings set just above the floor
- Stable anchor
- Optional parallettes as an intermediate step

## Difficulty

advanced

## Execution

1. Set rings low and even; assume a plank grip on the rings.
2. Create tension by slightly externally rotating/"breaking" the rings.
3. Lower the chest between the rings while keeping a rigid plank.
4. Descend only as deep as you can stabilize.
5. Press to full extension without losing ring control.

## Coaching Cues

- "Break the rings apart"
- "Body rigid like a plank"
- "Chest through, not hips sagging"
- "Smooth press, rings quiet"

## Common Mistakes

- Uneven ring height
- Hip sag or pike
- Collapsing into the shoulders
- Excessive depth beyond stability
- Uncontrolled elbow flare

## Breathing

Inhale on the way down; exhale on the press. Brace throughout.

## Range of Motion

Deepest stable ROM; do not chase depth at the expense of shoulder centering.

## Progressions

- More instability (lower rings/longer straps)
- Feet-elevated ring push-up
- Weighted vest
- Ring dip pathway

## Regressions

- Floor push-up
- Deficit push-up on stable handles
- Incline ring push-up
- Standard incline push-up

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 4–10 controlled reps

### Intensity

- RIR 2–4 early; progress toward RIR 1–2 as skill allows

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3 sessions weekly depending on shoulder recovery

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Effective when sets are stable; pair with stable presses if instability limits stimulus.

#### Strength

Builds pressing stability and relative strength.

#### Endurance

Not ideal until technique is consistent.

#### Fat Loss

Use only if form holds under fatigue.

## Contraindications

Inappropriate without solid floor push-up technique, or with symptomatic shoulder instability/pain. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Seated Cable Fly | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The seated cable fly uses a supported seat or bench between dual cables to reduce lower-body cheating while isolating the pectoralis major under continuous tension.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular musculature against the bench
- Reduced core demand versus standing

## Equipment

- Dual cable station
- Bench or seat positioned between stacks
- Handles

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Place a bench between cables; sit or lie supported as designed.
2. Start arms open with soft elbows.
3. Fly handles together to midline.
4. Return under control to stretch.
5. Keep upper back stable on the support.

## Coaching Cues

- "Supported back, soft elbows"
- "Hug to the midline"
- "Control the stretch"
- "No torso swing"

## Common Mistakes

- Bench placement causing asymmetric pull
- Pressing pattern
- Overstretch pain
- Using momentum from the hips

## Breathing

Exhale on squeeze; inhale on opening.

## Range of Motion

Comfortable stretch to midline squeeze.

## Progressions

- Load
- Standing cable fly
- Single-arm seated fly

## Regressions

Title: Single-Arm Dumbbell Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The single-arm dumbbell bench press loads one side at a time, increasing anti-rotation core demand and allowing unilateral strength/hypertrophy work to address side-to-side asymmetries.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Core anti-rotation musculature
- Scapular stabilizers
- Opposite-side trunk bracing

## Equipment

- One dumbbell
- Flat bench
- Free hand for bracing or light assistance as needed

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Lie on a flat bench with one dumbbell at the working shoulder.
2. Brace hard against rotation; non-working hand can hold the bench.
3. Press to lockout without twisting the torso off the bench.
4. Lower under control.
5. Complete prescribed reps, then switch sides.

## Coaching Cues

- "Brace like someone is pushing your ribs"
- "Hips and shoulders stay square"
- "Press without rotating"
- "Match depth side to side"

## Common Mistakes

- Allowing torso rotation
- Unequal ROM between sides
- Oversized load causing instability
- Shoulder dumping at the bottom

## Breathing

Exhale on press; inhale on lowering; maintain brace.

## Range of Motion

Same deep comfortable stretch as a bilateral dumbbell press.

## Progressions

- Heavier load
- Tempo eccentrics
- Pause reps

## Regressions

- Bilateral dumbbell press
- Machine single-arm press
- Landmine press

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets per side

### Reps

- 8–12

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 60–120 seconds between sides/sets

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Unilateral hypertrophy and asymmetry work.

#### Strength

Unilateral pressing strength.

#### Endurance

Moderate.

#### Fat Loss

Time-efficient if rest is managed.

## Contraindications

May be inappropriate during symptomatic anterior shoulder irritation, recent pectoralis or triceps strain, uncontrolled wrist/elbow pain, or when a safe setup/spot cannot be arranged. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Smith Machine Bench Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The Smith machine bench press is a rails-guided horizontal bar press. The fixed path reduces some balance demand and can allow confident loading, but it constrains natural bar path and may alter shoulder stress versus a free barbell. Treat it as a guided variation, not a perfect free-weight substitute.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Less whole-body stabilization than free barbell; scapular control still required

## Equipment

- Smith machine
- Flat bench aligned to mid-chest bar path
- Safety stops set appropriately

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Position the bench so the bar descends to mid-chest; set safeties.
2. Lie down, plant feet, and set the upper back.
3. Rotate to unhook; lower under control to the chest.
4. Press to extension without bouncing.
5. Re-hook securely before exiting.

## Coaching Cues

- "Bench placement first, then load"
- "Set safeties before heavy sets"
- "Touch with control"
- "Re-hook fully at the end"

## Common Mistakes

- Misaligned bench (bar path toward neck or belly)
- Ignoring safeties
- Excessive bouncing
- Forcing painful elbow angles on the fixed path
- Assuming the machine fixes technique errors

## Breathing

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

## Range of Motion

Touch the chest if comfortable. Shorten ROM or switch variations if the fixed path irritates the shoulders.

## Progressions

- Load increases
- Pause reps
- Tempo eccentrics
- Smith incline press

## Regressions

- Machine chest press
- Dumbbell bench press
- Push-up

## Programming

### Sets

- 3–4 sets

### Reps

- 6–12 typical

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 90–180 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–2 sessions weekly as press variety

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Useful guided overload tool for chest volume.

#### Strength

Can build pressing capacity; transfer to free barbell groove is imperfect.

#### Endurance

Moderate; other options may feel more natural at high reps.

#### Fat Loss

Acceptable compound when setup is quick and safe.

## Contraindications

Discontinue if the fixed path provokes sharp shoulder pain. Verify hooks/safeties. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Smith Machine Decline Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The Smith machine decline press combines a declined torso with a rails-guided bar path, often emphasizing sternal pectoralis fibers while providing safeties for guided overload.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major (sternal emphasis often increased)

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Scapular retractors; reduced free-bar stability demand

## Equipment

- Smith machine
- Decline bench aligned to lower/mid-chest touch
- Safety stops

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Secure legs on the decline bench under the Smith bar; align for lower/mid-chest contact.
2. Set safeties. Unhook the bar.
3. Lower under control to the chest.
4. Press to extension without bouncing.
5. Re-hook fully before exiting.

## Coaching Cues

- "Secure legs and safeties"
- "Lower-chest touch"
- "No bounce"
- "Re-hook completely"

## Common Mistakes

- Insecure decline setup
- Misaligned bench path
- Ignoring safeties
- Excessive bounce

## Breathing

Inhale on descent; exhale on press.

## Range of Motion

Touch lower/mid chest if comfortable; shorten if rails force painful angles.

## Progressions

- Load increases
- Pause reps
- Free-weight decline progressions when ready

## Regressions

- Decline dumbbell press
- Machine chest press
- High cable fly + flat press pairing

### Sets

- 6–12

- RIR 1–3

### Frequency

- 1–2x weekly

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Guided lower-chest biased overload.

Limited free-bar specificity.

Moderate.

Optional compound when setup is safe.

## Overview

## Overview

The squeeze press (hex/crush press) is a dumbbell press variation where the bells are pressed together throughout the ROM, increasing isometric adduction demand on the pectoralis major while still training the press pattern.

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

### Stabilizers

- Flat (or incline) bench

## Difficulty

intermediate

## Execution

1. Lie on a bench holding dumbbells together over the chest (hex ends touching if hexagonal).
2. Squeeze the dumbbells inward hard.
3. Press up while maintaining the squeeze.
4. Lower under control with continued inward pressure.
5. Do not let the bells separate.

## Coaching Cues

- "Crush the bells together"
- "Press and squeeze"
- "Control the descent"
- "Keep contact between bells"

- Losing inward pressure
- Excessive load that prevents squeeze
- Flaring and separating bells
- Partial unfinished lockouts

Inhale during the controlled eccentric (lowering). Brace the trunk, then exhale through the concentric press or near lockout. Avoid prolonged breath-holds on high-rep sets if dizziness occurs.

Full press ROM while dumbbells remain in contact.

- Heavier dumbbells with maintained squeeze

- Tempo work

Title: Svend Press | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The Svend press is a low-load chest isolation/activation drill performed by pressing plates together while extending the arms forward, emphasizing pectoralis major isometric adduction with a pressing component.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Anterior deltoids
- Triceps (minor)

### Stabilizers

- Scapular musculature
- Core in standing variations

## Equipment

- One or more weight plates pressed together
- Optional: standing or seated posture

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Press two plates (or a single plate with palms) together hard at mid-chest.
2. Maintain maximal inward squeeze.
3. Extend arms forward slowly while continuing the squeeze.
4. Return to the chest under squeeze tension.
5. Keep shoulders from elevating.

## Coaching Cues

- "Crush the plates together"
- "Arms extend, squeeze never stops"
- "Do not shrug"
- "Slow and deliberate"

## Common Mistakes

- Losing the squeeze and turning into a front raise
- Using too much load
- Shrugging
- Rushing reps

## Breathing

Steady breathing; exhale gently on extension.

## Range of Motion

From chest to near-full forward reach while squeeze is maintained.

## Progressions

- Slightly heavier plates
- Longer pauses at extension
- Cable squeeze press variations

## Regressions

- Isometric plate squeeze without press
- Pec deck light

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–3 sets

### Reps

- 10–20

### Intensity

- RIR 2–4; tension-focused

### Rest

- 45–75 seconds

### Frequency

- 1–3x weekly as activator/finisher

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Finisher/activation; not a primary mass builder.

#### Strength

Not for strength.

#### Endurance

Compatible with higher reps.

#### Fat Loss

Optional low-stress accessory.

## Contraindications

Stop if shoulder or wrist pain appears. Evidence for hypertrophy stimulus is limited versus loaded presses/flies. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

Title: Wall Push-Up | Category: exercise | Subcategory: chest

## Overview

## Overview

The wall push-up is the lightest common push-up regression, performed standing with hands on a wall. It teaches the horizontal press pattern with minimal load and is appropriate for absolute beginners or early return-to-pressing progressions.

## Muscles Worked

### Primary

- Pectoralis major

### Secondary

- Triceps brachii
- Anterior deltoids

### Stabilizers

- Trunk musculature (upright)

## Equipment

- Bodyweight
- Clear wall space

## Difficulty

beginner

## Execution

1. Stand facing a wall; place hands on the wall at roughly chest height and shoulder width.
2. Walk feet back to create a mild lean while keeping a straight body line.
3. Bend elbows to bring the chest toward the wall.
4. Press back to full elbow extension.
5. Progress by stepping feet farther back or moving to an incline push-up.

## Coaching Cues

- "Body in one line"
- "Chest to wall"
- "Full lockout"
- "Step farther back to progress"

## Common Mistakes

- Feet too close (almost no load)
- Sagging through the hips
- Partial range
- Hands far above head turning into a shoulder-dominant pattern

## Breathing

Inhale toward the wall; exhale as you press away.

## Range of Motion

Chest approaches the wall each rep; elbows extend fully on the press.

## Progressions

- Feet farther from the wall
- Incline push-up on a counter/bench
- Knee push-up
- Floor push-up

## Regressions

- Closer feet
- Smaller ROM if needed for comfort

## Programming

### Sets

- 2–4 sets

### Reps

- 8–15

### Intensity

- RIR 1–3

### Rest

- 45–75 seconds

### Frequency

- 2–4x weekly for beginners

### Best Goals

#### Hypertrophy

Entry hypertrophy stimulus when progressed.

#### Strength

Beginner pressing foundation.

#### Endurance

Easy higher-rep practice.

#### Fat Loss

Accessible low-stress pressing.

## Contraindications

Stop if wrist or shoulder pain appears; adjust hand height. This is training guidance, not medical diagnosis.

## Overview

intermediate

Inhale down; exhale up.

Chest to near-floor through controlled depth.
